title: What is it made of? Where every material comes from

summary.text: This unit is about where things come from. Every object is made of a material, the stuff it is made of. Every material began somewhere on Earth. It came from a plant, an animal, the rocks and soil, the sea or even the air. Some things are natural. Nature made them, like a stone, a mango or a crow's feather. Other things are made by people, like a steel spoon, a plastic bucket or a glass bangle. But people never make stuff out of nothing. They take natural raw materials and change them by cutting, spinning, melting, baking and mixing. Your child makes paper, salt, milk plastic, colour and a clay diya with their own hands. Then they zoom in. Natural and made things are built from the same tiny atoms, and those atoms were made long ago inside stars.
summary.art: A child holding a steel tumbler, with thin dotted lines running from it back to a hill with a mine, a cotton plant, a sheep, the sea with salt pans, and up into the night sky to a bright star.

intro.hook: Pick up anything near you. A pencil, a spoon, a button. Now ask it a question. Where were you before you were this? And before that? How far back can you go?
intro.text: Your pencil was once a tree. Its grey middle was once a rock deep in the ground. The tree drank rain that fell from clouds, and the rain came from the sea. Follow any object backwards, and you always end up at the Earth. In this unit you become a material detective. You trace things back to where they came from. You find out which things nature made and which things people made. Then you make a few made materials yourself, from natural ones.
intro.art: A pencil in the middle of a page, with a chain of small pictures leading back from it: a pencil factory, a log, a tree in rain, a cloud over the sea, and a second chain from the grey tip back to a dark rock in the ground.

outcomes: I can say what an object is made of, and trace its material back to where it came from: a plant, an animal, the ground, the sea or the air.
I can tell natural things from things made by people, and explain tricky ones like a wooden chair, a cotton kurta or a potted plant.
I can describe how people change natural raw materials into made materials, by cutting, spinning, melting, baking, mixing and heating.
I can make a made material from a natural one, like paper, salt, milk plastic, a dye or a clay diya. I can say what I think, what I saw and why.
I can explain that plants and animals make materials too, and that some made materials are copies of natural ones.
I can explain that natural and made things are built from the same kinds of atoms, and that those atoms were made long ago in stars.
I can say what scientists agree on and still argue about, and name some of the hidden people who dig, grow, spin and make our things.

terms.meaning: A thing you can see, touch and use. A tumbler, a chair and a kite are all objects.
terms.example: A spoon is an object. You can hold it and eat with it.
terms.art: A steel tumbler, a wooden chair and a paper kite in a row.

terms.meaning: The stuff an object is made of. One material can make many objects. One object can be made of many materials.
terms.example: A tumbler can be made of steel, glass or plastic. A school bag is cloth, plastic and metal together.
terms.art: Three tumblers in a row: steel, glass and plastic.

terms.meaning: Made by nature, not by people. A natural thing can be living, like a tree or a bird. It can be non-living, like a rock, water or air.
terms.example: A neem tree, a pebble and rainwater are all natural.
terms.art: A neem tree, a pebble and raindrops in one sunny scene.

terms.meaning: Made by people from other materials. Scientists and books also call it artificial, human-made or manufactured.
terms.example: A steel spoon, a brick, a plastic bucket and a cotton kurta are all made by people.
terms.art: A brick, a plastic bucket and a steel spoon on a shelf, with a pair of hands beside them.

terms.meaning: A natural material before people change it. It is the starting stuff.
terms.example: Cotton fluff is the raw material for cotton thread. Clay is the raw material for a brick.
terms.art: A fluffy white cotton boll on its plant, next to a lump of wet clay.

terms.meaning: The place a material comes from.
terms.example: The source of wool is a sheep. The source of salt is the sea.
terms.art: A sheep and a wave of sea water, each with an arrow to a ball of wool and a heap of salt.

terms.meaning: A rock with a metal hidden inside it. People dig it out of the ground and heat it until the metal comes out.
terms.example: Iron ore is a reddish rock. It is dug from mines in Odisha, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh.
terms.art: A chunk of reddish iron ore next to a shiny iron nail.

terms.meaning: A long, thin thread that grows inside or on a plant. People spin plant fibres into thread and rope.
terms.example: Cotton, jute and coir from coconut husks are plant fibres.
terms.art: Three bundles: white cotton, golden jute and brown coconut coir.

terms.meaning: To twist short fibres together into one long, strong thread.
terms.example: A charkha, a spinning wheel, twists cotton fluff into thread.
terms.art: A child's hands twisting cotton fluff into a thin thread.

terms.meaning: To cross threads over and under each other to make cloth.
terms.example: A weaver on a handloom weaves thread into a sari.
terms.art: Threads going over and under each other on a simple loom.

terms.meaning: A very hot oven for baking clay. Baking makes soft clay into hard pottery and bricks.
terms.example: Bricks are baked in a brick kiln with a tall chimney.
terms.art: A brick kiln with a tall chimney and stacks of red bricks.

terms.meaning: A very hot fire inside a closed chamber. It is hot enough to melt sand into glass, or ore into metal.
terms.example: Glass bangles in Firozabad are made from glass melted in furnaces.
terms.art: An orange glowing furnace mouth with a worker holding a long rod of hot glass.

terms.meaning: A thick, dark oil found deep under the ground and the sea floor. It formed over millions of years from tiny sea living things. Most plastic is made from it, and from natural gas.
terms.example: Petrol for scooters and the plastic of a bucket both come from petroleum.
terms.art: A layer of dark oil in rocks deep underground, with tiny sea creatures drawn in the rock above it.

terms.meaning: A made material that can be shaped when it is soft and warm, then sets hard. Most plastic is made from petroleum and natural gas.
terms.example: Buckets, toothbrushes and pens are usually plastic.
terms.art: A red plastic bucket, a toothbrush and a pen.

terms.meaning: Made by people through chemistry, by joining or changing tiny bits of other materials.
terms.example: Nylon and polyester are synthetic fibres. Cotton and silk are natural fibres.
terms.art: A nylon rope beside a cotton rope.

terms.meaning: The steps people use to change a raw material into something useful.
terms.example: Clay is dug, mixed with water, shaped, dried and baked. That is the process for making a pot.
terms.art: Five small pictures in a row: digging clay, mixing, shaping on a wheel, drying, baking.

terms.meaning: A coloured material that soaks into cloth and colours it.
terms.example: Turmeric dyes cloth yellow. Indigo dyes it blue.
terms.art: Three strips of cloth: yellow from turmeric, pink from beetroot and blue from indigo.

terms.meaning: To break down an old made thing and use its material to make a new thing.
terms.example: Old newspapers can be soaked, mashed and made into new paper.
terms.art: A pile of old newspapers turning, through arrows, into a fresh sheet of handmade paper.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that everything is made of. Atoms are far too small to see, even with a microscope.
terms.example: A wooden spoon, a plastic spoon and your hand are all made of atoms.
terms.art: A zoom from a spoon, to a speck, to a cluster of tiny coloured balls.

terms.meaning: One pure kind of atom. There are about 90 kinds found in nature. Every material in the world is made from them.
terms.example: Carbon, oxygen, iron and gold are elements.
terms.art: A small grid of coloured squares, each with an element symbol, like a mini periodic table.

terms.meaning: An element found in every living thing. Wood, cotton, sugar, plastic, pencil lead and you are full of carbon atoms.
terms.example: The grey stuff in your pencil is almost pure carbon.
terms.art: A pencil tip, a sugar cube and a leaf, all with a small black carbon atom drawn beside them.

terms.meaning: A name for the atoms that were made inside stars long ago and spread into space. The atoms in you and your things are stardust.
terms.example: Most of the oxygen and carbon in your body was made inside stars that exploded or puffed off their outer layers before the Sun was born.
terms.art: A child with arms wide, sparkles drifting down from an exploding star high above.

terms.meaning: To be broken down slowly by tiny living things, like bacteria and fungi, back into soil and air.
terms.example: A fallen leaf decomposes into soil in a few months.
terms.art: A leaf on soil in four stages, from whole to crumbly to gone.

explanations.concept: Every object is made of a material
explanations.definition: An object is a thing. A material is the stuff it is made of. The same material can make many objects, and one object can be made of many materials.
explanations.description: Ask 'What is it?' and you get the object. Ask 'What is it made of?' and you get the material. A tumbler is an object. Steel is its material. Many objects are made of more than one material. Each part has its own job. A pressure cooker has a metal body, a rubber ring and a plastic handle. The unit on Properties of materials explores why each part needs its own material.
examples: A wooden spoon and a wooden door are made of the same material.
A pencil is wood outside and grey graphite, a kind of carbon, inside.
A school bag is cloth, a plastic zip and a metal buckle.
explanations.art: A pressure cooker with three labels: metal body, rubber ring, plastic handle.
explanations.context: This card explains the first idea of the unit: the difference between an object and the material it is made of.

explanations.definition: Every material comes from somewhere on Earth. Most come from plants, from animals, or from the ground. Some come from the sea or even the air.
explanations.description: Follow any material back far enough, and you reach a source in nature. Wood, cotton, jute, rubber and paper come from plants. Wool, silk, leather, honey and lac come from animals. Stone, clay, sand, metals and oil come from the ground. Salt comes mostly from the sea. Even the air is a source. Factories take nitrogen out of the air to make fertiliser for farms. Nothing that people make comes from nowhere.
examples: Paper comes from trees, or from old paper.
Glass comes mostly from sand.
A rubber band comes from the milky sap of a rubber tree, grown in Kerala and the north-east.
A silk sari comes from the cocoon of a silkworm.
explanations.art: A big circle with five pictures around the edge, a tree, a sheep, a hill with a mine, the sea and the sky, each with arrows to objects in the middle.
explanations.context: Where did your things come from before they reached the shop? This card names the five big sources of every material.

explanations.definition: Natural things are made by nature. They can be living, like a tree, or non-living, like a rock or water. Things made by people are called artificial, or human-made.
explanations.description: A mango, a crow, a pebble and the wind are natural. Nobody made them. A bicycle, a brick and a plastic bottle are made by people. Here is the tricky part. Every made thing is made from natural things. A wooden chair is made by people, from a natural material, wood. So we ask two questions. First, what is the material? Second, did people make this thing from it?
examples: A cotton boll on the plant is natural. A cotton kurta is made by people from it.
A potted plant is natural. The pot is made by people.
A cement road is made by people, from natural limestone, clay and sand.
explanations.art: Two columns of pictures: a mango tree, a crow and a pebble on one side, a bicycle, a brick and a plastic bottle on the other, a wooden chair standing on the line between them.
explanations.context: This card explains the two big groups of things in the world: natural things, and things made by people.

explanations.definition: People change raw materials by cutting, shaping, spinning, weaving, melting, baking, mixing and heating. The steps are called a process.
explanations.description: Some materials are changed only a little. A carpenter cuts and shapes wood, but it is still wood. Others are changed a lot. Clay baked in a kiln becomes hard pottery that never turns back into clay. Sand melted in a furnace becomes glass. Ore heated with charcoal or coke gives out metal. Petroleum is changed in a factory into tiny plastic beads. These are melted and pressed into buckets. The more fire a process needs, the more the material usually changes.
examples: Cotton is picked, cleaned, spun into thread and woven into cloth.
Clay is dug, mixed with water, shaped, dried and baked into a matka.
Sand is mixed with soda ash and limestone, melted, and blown or pressed into glass.
explanations.art: Three journey chains drawn as arrows: cotton plant to kurta, clay to matka, sand to glass bangle.
explanations.context: Made things start as natural things. This card shows the main ways people change them.

explanations.description: Everyone agrees on the easy cases. A pebble is natural, and a plastic bucket is made by people. But where exactly is the line? Thinkers give different answers.
examples: Plastic is made from oil, and oil formed from tiny sea living things that died millions of years ago.
A beaver's dam is built by an animal. A farmer's mud dam is built by people. Are both natural?

perspectives.who: The everyday view, used in most school books
perspectives.explanation: If people made it or changed it a lot, it is made by people, or artificial. Otherwise it is natural.

What matters is the substance, not who made it. Indigo dye made in a factory is the very same substance as indigo from the plant. So a material can be both made by people and exactly like a natural one.

People are animals and part of nature. Birds build nests and termites build towers. So perhaps a city is as natural as an anthill. Others reply that people change the Earth far more than any other animal, so the word 'artificial' still helps.

explanations.art: An anthill, a bird's nest and a city skyline side by side, with a question mark above them.
explanations.context: This card is about a puzzle with no single answer: where nature stops and people begin.

explanations.definition: Many animals make materials. Some grow them on their bodies, and some build with them.
explanations.description: A sheep grows wool, and people only cut it. A silkworm, the caterpillar of a moth, spins a cocoon of one long silk thread. Bees make wax for their honeycomb. In Jharkhand and nearby states, tiny lac insects on trees make a resin. People scrape it off to make bangles, varnish and sealing wax. Spiders spin silk that is very strong for its weight. Paper wasps chew wood and spit it out as paper for their nests. In 1719 a French scientist, René Réaumur, watched these wasps. He wrote that people could learn to make paper from wood, as wasps do. About 120 years later, people did.
examples: Wool from sheep, silk from silkworms, honey and wax from bees.
Lac from lac insects makes the shiny red lac bangles of Rajasthan.
A weaver bird weaves its nest from strips of grass.
explanations.art: A paper wasp nest hanging from a branch, a silkworm cocoon, and a lac insect crust on a twig.
explanations.context: People are not the only makers. This card is about materials that animals make.

explanations.concept: Plants are built of a material called cellulose
explanations.definition: Cellulose is the stuff that plant walls are made of. Wood, cotton, jute, coir and paper are mostly cellulose.
explanations.description: Every plant is made of tiny boxes called cells. The walls of these cells are made of cellulose. It is made of long chains of sugar joined end to end. Cotton is almost pure cellulose. Wood is cellulose glued together with another plant stuff. Scientists think there is more cellulose on Earth than any other material made by living things. When you make paper in this unit, you are tangling cellulose fibres into a mat.
examples: Cotton fluff is nearly pure cellulose.
Paper is a mat of cellulose fibres pressed flat.
Cows can digest grass because tiny living things in their stomach break cellulose down.
explanations.art: A zoom from a leaf, to rows of box-shaped plant cells, to a long chain of sugar beads in one wall.
explanations.context: Many of our materials come from plants. This card zooms in to find what plants are made of.

explanations.concept: Materials from deep in the ground: metals, sand, clay and oil
explanations.definition: Metals come from ores, rocks with metal inside. Glass comes from sand. Bricks and pots come from clay. Most plastic comes from petroleum and natural gas.
explanations.description: Metals hide inside ores. People dig the ore out of mines and heat it in a furnace until the metal comes out. Clay is soil made of very tiny grains. It becomes sticky when wet, and hard when baked. Petroleum is a thick, dark oil from deep underground. It formed over millions of years from tiny living things in ancient seas. They were buried in mud and slowly squeezed and warmed. So plastic is made from living things that died long before the dinosaurs.
examples: Bauxite, a reddish ore from Odisha and other states, gives aluminium for pressure cookers.
Sand from riverbeds and quarries is melted into glass.
A plastic bucket started as oil pumped up from deep underground or under the sea.
explanations.art: A cut-away picture of the ground: a mine with iron ore near the top, a layer of clay, and deep down a layer of dark oil, with tiny ancient sea creatures drawn in the rock.
explanations.context: Many materials come from under our feet. This card follows four of them up out of the ground.

explanations.concept: The first made materials that copied nature
explanations.definition: Some made materials were invented to copy natural ones, or to take their place. Often they are made by chemistry, so they are called synthetic.
explanations.description: In 1862 Alexander Parkes, in England, made one of the first plastics from cotton cellulose. In 1907 Leo Baekeland, in the United States, made Bakelite. It was the first plastic made completely from chemicals, not from plants or animals. Old black telephones and radio cases were made of it. In 1935 Wallace Carothers and his team made nylon. People used it in place of silk for stockings and ropes. In 1856 an English teenager, William Perkin, made the first synthetic dye by accident. He was trying to make a medicine.
examples: Nylon took the place of silk for many things.
Rayon is made from wood pulp. It was once called 'artificial silk'.
Lab-grown diamonds are real diamond, made by people from carbon.
explanations.art: A timeline with four pictures: a Parkesine comb in 1862, a Bakelite telephone in 1907, a nylon rope in 1935, and a purple cloth dyed with Perkin's colour in 1856 at the start.
explanations.context: Some made materials copy natural ones. This card tells how a few of them were first made.

explanations.concept: Blue from a plant, blue from a factory: the story of indigo
explanations.definition: Indigo is a blue dye. It used to come only from plants. Since 1897 it has also been made in factories, and the factory indigo is the very same substance.
explanations.description: For thousands of years, India was famous for indigo. It was made from the leaves of the indigo plant. In the 1800s, British planters forced many farmers in Bengal and Bihar to grow indigo instead of food. The farmers were paid very little. In 1859 and 1860, indigo farmers in Bengal rose up against the planters. In 1878 a German chemist, Adolf von Baeyer, worked out how to make indigo from chemicals. In 1897 a German company began selling factory indigo. It was cheaper, so plant indigo collapsed. In 1917, a farmer called Rajkumar Shukla persuaded Gandhi to come to Champaran in Bihar. He came to support the indigo farmers. Today almost all the blue in jeans is factory indigo.
examples: Blue jeans are dyed with indigo.
Some craftspeople in India still dye with plant indigo.
explanations.art: Split picture: on the left, women steeping green indigo leaves in a tank of blue water, on the right, a factory pouring the same blue into a vat, a pair of blue jeans in the middle.
explanations.context: Can a made material be exactly the same as a natural one? This card tells the true story of a blue dye.

explanations.concept: Zoom in: the same tiny bricks build everything
explanations.definition: Everything, natural or made, is built from atoms. There are about 90 kinds of atom found in nature, called elements.
explanations.description: Imagine a box of building blocks with about 90 colours. With them you can build anything at all. Atoms work like that. Wood, cotton, sugar and plastic are all made mostly of just three elements: carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. They are different because the atoms are joined in different patterns. A diamond and the grey in your pencil are both pure carbon, joined in different ways. When people make a material, they never make new atoms. They only move atoms around and join them in new ways.
examples: A wooden spoon and a plastic spoon are both mostly carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
Diamond and pencil graphite are both pure carbon.
Water is two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom.
explanations.art: Two piles of the same coloured beads: one built into a wooden spoon shape, one built into a plastic bottle shape.
explanations.context: This card zooms in, far past anything a microscope can show. It finds out what all materials are made of deep down.

explanations.concept: Where atoms come from: made in stars
explanations.description: Scientists agree on most of this story. Right after the universe began, there was almost only hydrogen and helium, the two lightest elements. Stars are giant furnaces. Inside them, light atoms are squeezed together into heavier ones, like carbon, oxygen and iron. When big stars die, they blow these atoms out into space. New stars and planets, like our Sun and Earth, form from that dust. So the iron in your spoon was made in a star. The open question is about the heaviest atoms, like gold.
examples: The carbon in your pencil was made inside a star.
The iron in your blood and in a kadhai was made in stars.

perspectives.explanation: Gold and other heavy atoms were made mostly in supernovas, the giant explosions of dying big stars.

In 2017, telescopes watched two dead stars, called neutron stars, crash together. The crash threw out heavy atoms, perhaps including gold. So many scientists now think crashes like this make much of the gold.
Crashes alone may not explain all the gold, especially in the oldest stars. Some rare kinds of exploding star may make it too. The answer is still being worked out.

explanations.art: A big star exploding, spraying coloured sparks labelled carbon, oxygen and iron, two small bright stars crashing in a corner, spraying gold sparks.
explanations.context: If everything is made of atoms, where did the atoms come from? This card follows them back to the stars.

explanations.concept: Hidden hands: the people inside our things
explanations.definition: Every made thing passes through many people's hands, from the field or the mine to the shop.
explanations.description: Think of a cotton kurta. A farmer grew the cotton, often in great heat. Pickers picked it by hand. Workers in a mill cleaned and spun it. A weaver wove it. A tailor stitched it. Drivers carried it at every step. Most of these people are never named. Some were paid very little. Long ago, the cloth of Bengal, called Dhaka muslin, was so fine it was famous across the world. It was spun by hand from a special cotton plant. The skill was lost in the 1800s. Today people in Bangladesh are trying to bring it back. In 1930 Gandhi asked Indians to spin their own thread on a charkha. He said it showed that people could make their own things.
examples: A steel spoon passed through the hands of miners, furnace workers and factory workers.
Recycled paper and plastic in India are often collected by kabadiwalas and waste pickers, many of them women.
explanations.art: A cotton kurta in the middle, ringed by small portraits: a farmer, a picker, a spinner, a weaver, a tailor and a truck driver.
explanations.context: A made thing is not only stuff. This card is about the people whose work is hidden inside it.

explanations.concept: People are now changing the Earth's materials
explanations.description: In 2020, scientists in Israel added up the weight of everything people have made. That means buildings, roads, machines and plastic. They found it now weighs about as much as all the living things on Earth put together. In 1900 it weighed only about 3 parts for every 100 parts of living things. Scientists have also found a new kind of rock on a beach in Hawaii, made of melted plastic, sand and stones. So some scientists asked: should we name a new age of the Earth after people?
examples: New rocks of melted plastic and stone, called plastiglomerate, were described in 2014.
Concrete is the made material people use most, after water.

perspectives.explanation: People now change the Earth so much that we live in a new age. Some call it the Anthropocene, which means 'the age of humans'.

perspectives.who: The scientists who officially name Earth's ages, in 2024
perspectives.explanation: They voted not to name the Anthropocene as an official age, for now. Some said the start date was not clear. Others said the idea is still useful, even if it is not official.

explanations.art: A pan balance: one side piled with buildings, roads, cars and plastic, the other side with trees, whales, people and insects, the two sides nearly level.
explanations.context: This card is about how much stuff people have made, and a new rock found on a beach.

agreed.text: Every material comes from a source on Earth: plants, animals, the ground, the sea or the air.
agreed.evidence: Every material we know can be traced back to one of these. People have followed these journeys in mines, fields and factories for thousands of years.

agreed.text: Made things are made from natural raw materials, changed by people.
agreed.evidence: You can watch it happen. Clay becomes a pot in a kiln. Cotton becomes thread on a charkha. Old paper becomes new paper in your own kitchen.

agreed.text: People do not make new atoms when they make materials. They join atoms in new ways.
agreed.evidence: Chemists have weighed what goes into and comes out of their work for over 200 years. The French chemist Antoine Lavoisier, helped by Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, showed in the 1700s that nothing is lost or created, only changed.

agreed.text: A made substance can be exactly the same as a natural one.
agreed.evidence: Factory indigo and plant indigo give the same results in every chemical test. Lab-grown diamonds and mined diamonds are both pure carbon in the same pattern.

agreed.text: The atoms in everything around us were made in stars, except for most of the hydrogen.
agreed.evidence: Telescopes split the light of stars into colours, and each element leaves its own pattern of colours. These show which atoms stars hold, and how stars make them.

challenging.claim: Natural things are always safe and good. Made things are always harmful.
challenging.who: A common belief, often used in adverts
challenging.for: Some made things, like plastic waste and some chemicals, do harm living things.
challenging.against: Many natural things are poisonous, like dhatura seeds or snake venom. Asbestos is a natural rock fibre that harms lungs. Many made things save lives, like medicines and clean water pipes. We have to ask about each thing, not about where it came from.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that 'natural' means good and 'made' means bad.

challenging.claim: Plastic is completely unnatural. It has nothing to do with nature.
challenging.for: Plastic is made in factories, by people, through chemistry. Nothing like most plastics is found in nature.
challenging.against: Plastic is made from petroleum and natural gas. These formed from tiny living things in ancient seas. So plastic is made by people, but from a natural raw material. Its atoms are ordinary carbon and hydrogen.
challenging.context: This card asks where plastic really comes from.

challenging.claim: Cotton cloth was first made in Europe or China.
challenging.who: Some older history books written outside India
challenging.for: Europe and China had great cloth-makers. England's mills made huge amounts of cotton cloth in the 1800s.
challenging.against: The oldest cotton threads found anywhere were found at Mehrgarh, in present-day Pakistan, wound around a copper bead about 8,000 years old. Cotton cloth was made in the Indus Valley more than 4,000 years ago. For centuries, the finest cotton cloth in the world came from India.
challenging.context: This card is about where cotton cloth was first made.

challenging.claim: A diamond made in a laboratory is a fake diamond.
challenging.who: Some jewellery sellers and many shoppers
challenging.for: Mined diamonds took millions or billions of years to form deep in the Earth. Lab diamonds take only weeks.
challenging.against: A lab diamond is made of carbon atoms in exactly the same pattern as a mined diamond. Experts need special machines to tell them apart. It is a real diamond that was made by people. A fake would be glass or another stone pretending to be a diamond.
challenging.context: This card asks whether a diamond made by people is a real diamond.

challenging.claim: Recycling solves the problem of made materials we throw away.
challenging.for: Recycling turns old paper, metal and some plastic into new things, and saves raw materials.
challenging.against: In 2017, three scientists, Roland Geyer, Jenna Jambeck and Kara Lavender Law, counted all the plastic waste ever made. Only about 9 parts in every 100 had been recycled. Most was buried or ended up on land and in the sea. Scientists agree recycling helps, but most say using less and reusing more matter too.
challenging.context: This card is about whether recycling is enough.

challenging.who: A common way of talking: 'nature' means places without people
challenging.for: People change the Earth far more than any other animal. Cities, plastic and new rocks look very different from forests.
challenging.against: People are living things, made of the same atoms as every other living thing. We breathe, eat and die like other animals. Many Adivasi and other traditions have long said that people belong to nature, not outside it. Scientists and philosophers still argue about how best to say this.
challenging.context: This card asks whether people are part of nature or separate from it.

big_questions.q: Is there anything in your home that did not come from the Earth?
big_questions.hint: Trace the strangest thing you can find back to its source. Where do you end up?

big_questions.q: If every made thing is made from natural things, is anything really unnatural?
big_questions.hint: Is a bird's nest natural? Is a house? What is the difference?

big_questions.q: The atoms in your body were made in stars. Does that make you a little bit of a star?
big_questions.hint: Your iron, your carbon and your oxygen were all made in stars long ago.

big_questions.q: Who owns the sea's salt, the river's sand, or the iron in a hill?
big_questions.hint: Think of the people who live near them, the people who dig them, and the people who sell them.

big_questions.q: When people make a material, they never make new atoms. So what exactly do they make?
big_questions.hint: Think of building blocks. Is a tower made of something new, or of the same blocks in a new pattern?

big_questions.q: Your kurta passed through many hands before it reached you. Should we know their names?
big_questions.hint: Who grew it, spun it, wove it and stitched it?

big_questions.q: Is a made copy of a natural thing worth less than the natural one?
big_questions.hint: Think of factory indigo, a lab diamond, or a photo of a painting.

big_questions.q: Animals like wasps and silkworms make materials. What else might we learn from them?
big_questions.hint: Wasps were making paper long before people learned to make it from wood.

big_questions.q: Should we choose things made from materials that can go back to the Earth?
big_questions.hint: What happens to a clay kulhad after you drink chai from it? What happens to a plastic cup?

big_questions.q: Where is 'away', when we throw something away?
big_questions.hint: Every material has to go somewhere.

big_questions.q: Could people one day make materials from things in space, like rocks on the Moon?
big_questions.hint: Moon dust has oxygen and metals in it. Some space agencies are testing ways to use it.

story.title: The Salt in the Stone Hollow
story.note: The Salt March is real. From 12 March to 6 April 1930, Gandhi and 78 marchers walked about 385 kilometres from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi, on the coast of Gujarat. At Dandi he picked up a lump of salty mud, breaking the British law that forbade Indians to collect or make salt. Accounts say salt deposits on the shore had been trampled into the mud before he arrived. In the weeks after, people across India, many of them women, made salt. Kashi, her grandmother and the stone hollows are made up.
text: In the village where Kashi lived, on the coast of Gujarat, the sea came in twice a day and went out twice a day. Each time it went, it left something behind.

Kashi's grandmother, whom everyone called Ba, knew a place among the black rocks where the sea left the most. There were little hollows in the stone, round as cupped hands. At high tide the sea filled them. At low tide the water stayed behind, warm and still, while the sun stared down at it.
'Don't go to the hollows,' Ba told her. 'Not this month. The salt man is walking the shore.'

The salt man wore a khaki uniform and carried a stick. His job was to make sure nobody took the salt. In 1930 the law said that salt belonged to the British government. Only the government could collect it or sell it, and it added a tax to the price. Kashi's family bought salt from the shop in a twist of paper. It cost more than it should, for something so plain.

Kashi had always imagined that the government made the salt. She pictured a great building somewhere, with chimneys and fires and machines, pouring out white grains. That was why it cost money. That was why it was theirs.

Then the news came along the road, from village to village, faster than any bus. An old man was walking from Ahmedabad to the sea. He had nearly eighty people walking with him, and every day more joined. He was coming to make salt.

In the village, people laughed. 'Make salt?' said the shopkeeper. 'With what? He has no factory. He has a walking stick and a shawl.' Kashi laughed too, a little. You could not make salt by walking. You needed fire and machines.
But that afternoon, when the salt man had gone home for his lunch, Kashi slipped down to the black rocks.

She knelt beside the biggest hollow. The water in it was low, much lower than at high tide. All around its edge there was a white rim, like frost on a winter window. She touched it. It was crisp. She touched her finger to her tongue. Salt.

Kashi sat there a long time. The sun was hot on her neck. She watched the water. She could not see it moving, but she knew it was going somewhere. Each time she looked, the white rim had crept a little further in. Tiny white squares were growing on the surface, like boats, and sinking, and new ones growing.
Nobody was making this salt.

There was no chimney and no machine. There was only the sea, and the sun, and the stone. The salt had been in the sea all along, hidden in the water the way sugar hides in tea. The sun took the water away into the air, a little at a time. What was left behind was salt. All a person had to do was wait, and then pick it up.

Kashi stood up so fast that her knees cracked. If nobody made salt, then nobody had a right to sell it as if they had made it. The government had not made the sea. It had not made the sun. It had only put a man with a stick between the people and the shore.
She ran home and told Ba. Ba did not laugh. She only nodded slowly, as if she had known it for seventy years and had been waiting for someone to say it out loud.

The marchers reached Dandi, further down the coast, at the beginning of April. Kashi's father walked there, and Kashi walked beside him, and half the village came too. The shore was crowded. There were people sitting on the dunes, and people standing in the shallow water, and people singing.

Early on the morning of the sixth of April, after a prayer, the old man walked down to the shore. Kashi could see that the white crust had been broken up and trampled into the mud by many boots. Someone had tried to hide the salt.
The old man bent down. He picked up a lump of salty mud in his hand and held it up.

That was all. It was so small. A lump of mud. Somebody near Kashi breathed out, and somebody else began to cry. Kashi understood. He had not made salt. Nobody could make salt. He had only picked up what the sea had left for everyone.

In the weeks that followed, the salt men could not walk every shore. Women carried brass plates and clay pots down to the water in towns and villages all along the coast. They filled them with sea water and set them in the sun on their rooftops. Kashi's mother did it. Ba did it, sitting on the rocks with her sari tucked up, not hiding at all.

Kashi set out a plate of her own, on the flat stone by their door. All day she watched it. The water shrank. The white rim crept inwards. By the evening the plate was a ring of salt, glittering, like a small full moon that had come down to stay.
She did not sell it. She gave a pinch to everyone who passed.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the turn of the story is Kashi's discovery that salt is a natural material. People do not make it. The sea already holds it, and the sun takes away the water, leaving the salt behind. People only collect it. This is the heart of the unit: made things are natural things that people collect and change, and nobody makes stuff from nothing. The story also asks who can own a natural material, and shows the many ordinary people, many of them women, who made salt in 1930.
ask: At first, where did Kashi think salt came from? What did she find out at the stone hollow?
Where was the salt before it appeared on the rim of the hollow?
The old man picked up a lump of salty mud. Why did that small thing matter so much?
Is salt from the sea natural, or made by people? What do people do to it?
Who do you think should own the salt in the sea?

games.title: Back to the Earth: a card game of journeys
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: This is a card game about where materials come from. You collect sets of three cards: a natural source, the raw material, and a made thing. Together they show one material's journey.

printables.title: 36 journey cards to cut out: 12 sets of 3 (source, raw material, made thing)
items: RAW: coir fibre from the husk

rules: Cut out all the cards. Put the 6 HOW cards face up in the middle.
Shuffle the 36 journey cards. Deal 5 to each player. Put the rest face down as a pile.
On your turn, ask one player for a card you need. For example: 'Do you have the RAW card for the glass bangle?'
If they have it, they give it to you. If not, they say 'Dig!' and you take a card from the pile.
When you have a full set of three, lay it down in order: source, raw, made. Read the journey out loud.
Then take the HOW card that fits your journey, and say how people change the raw material. A correct HOW wins 1 extra point.
A full set is worth 3 points. When the pile runs out, the player with the most points wins.

flow.context: This is the first step of Back to the Earth, a card game where you collect the three steps of a material's journey.
flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Put the 6 HOW cards face up in the middle. 3. Shuffle the journey cards and deal 5 to each player. 4. Put the rest face down in a pile.
flow.say: Every made thing has a journey. It starts at a source in nature, like a plant, an animal or a mine. Then it becomes a raw material. Then people change it into a thing. In this game, you collect whole journeys.
flow.kid: Every made thing has a journey. It starts in nature. Collect all three steps: source, raw, made. Let's deal the cards.

flow.do: Play one practice set together. Find the cards 'SOURCE: the sea', 'RAW: sea water' and 'MADE: packet of salt'. Lay them in order.
flow.say: Here is one journey. The sea, then sea water, then a packet of salt. Which HOW card fits? How do people get salt from sea water?
flow.kid: Practice set: the sea, sea water, a packet of salt. Which HOW card fits? Tap it.

check.q: How do people get salt out of sea water?
options: Bake it in a kiln
Dry it in the sun
Spin and weave it
check.why: Sea water has salt dissolved in it. In salt pans, the sun takes the water away into the air, and the salt is left behind. Picking 'bake it in a kiln' usually means thinking every made thing needs a big fire. Some, like salt, need only sunshine and time.

flow.do: 1. Take turns asking for cards. 2. When someone makes a set, they lay it down, read the journey out loud and choose a HOW card. 3. Everyone checks whether the HOW is right.
flow.say: When you lay down a set, tell us the whole journey. Then tell us how people changed the raw material.
flow.kid: Ask for the cards you need. Got all three? Lay them down. Read the journey out loud. Then pick the HOW card.
flow.parent: Good HOWs: cotton, wool and silk are spun and woven. Wood pulp is mashed and pressed flat into paper. Sand is melted in a furnace into glass. Iron ore is melted in a furnace to get iron. Clay is baked in a kiln. Sea water is dried in the sun. Latex and petroleum are heated and moulded. Wax is melted and moulded too. Accept a good reason even if it is not on a card.

ask.q: Which journeys start with a living thing?
good: Cotton, wool, silk, wood, rubber, coconut and beeswax.

flow.do: Count the points. Then lay all the sets out together and sort them into three groups: from plants, from animals, from the ground or sea.
flow.say: Look at all the journeys. Which ones began with a plant? Which with an animal? Which with the ground or the sea? Was there any journey that did not start in nature?
flow.kid: Count your points. Now sort the sets. Plants, animals, or ground and sea. Did any journey start somewhere else?
flow.think: The plastic bucket started at an oil well. But where did the oil come from, long, long ago?

setup.caption: 1. Deal 5 cards each. Put the HOW cards in the middle.

setup.caption: 2. Ask for the card you need to finish a journey.

games.title: Who Made It? The Tricky Court
games.players: 3 or more players: one judge and two or more lawyers. Or one child and one grown-up taking turns.
games.context: This is an arguing game. Each card shows a tricky thing. Players argue whether nature made it, an animal made it, or people made it. A judge decides.

printables.title: 20 tricky case cards
items: A cultured pearl, grown in an oyster on a pearl farm
A diamond made in a laboratory
A rock made of melted plastic, sand and stones, found on a beach

rules: Choose one judge. Lay out the three court mats.
The judge reads a case card out loud.
Each lawyer chooses a mat and argues for it in two or three sentences. Each must give a reason.
The judge puts the card on the mat with the best reason. That lawyer wins a gavel token.
If the case is truly tricky, the judge can put it on the line between two mats. Then both lawyers win a token.
Swap judges every 5 cards. The player with the most tokens wins.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Tricky Court, a game where you argue about who made something: nature, an animal or people.
flow.do: 1. Lay out the three mats: MADE BY NATURE, MADE BY AN ANIMAL and MADE BY PEOPLE. 2. Shuffle the case cards. 3. Choose the first judge.
flow.say: Natural things are made by nature. Some are made by animals. Other things are made by people, from natural materials. Some things are tricky. Today you are lawyers. You must argue who made each thing, with a reason.
flow.kid: You are a lawyer today! Each card is a tricky thing. Who made it? Nature, an animal, or people? Give a reason.

flow.do: Play the first case together: 'A cultured pearl, grown in an oyster on a pearl farm.'
flow.say: On a pearl farm, people put a tiny bead inside an oyster. The oyster then coats it with pearl, layer by layer, for a year or more. So who made the pearl?
flow.kid: People put a tiny bead in an oyster. The oyster coats it with pearl. Who made the pearl?

check.q: A cultured pearl. Who made it?
options: Only people
Only the oyster
Both: the oyster made the pearl, but people started it
check.why: The oyster made every layer of the pearl. But people put the bead inside and looked after the oyster. So it is a good tricky case, and the line between natural and made is not always sharp. Picking 'only people' usually means thinking a farm makes everything on it. Picking 'only the oyster' leaves out the farmer's part. This is a game moment, so any well-argued answer can win.

flow.do: 1. The judge reads each card. 2. Lawyers argue. 3. The judge places the card and gives a token. 4. Swap judges every 5 cards.
flow.say: Judge, read the case. Lawyers, make your case. Remember to give a reason.
flow.kid: Judge reads a card. Lawyers argue. Judge decides. Win a token for a good reason.
flow.parent: Helpful facts for the judge. A paper wasp's nest really is paper, made by the wasp from chewed wood. Honey is made by bees from flower nectar. A loaf of bread is made by people, from wheat and with the help of yeast, a tiny living thing. Rain and sand dunes are natural. A cement road is made by people from natural limestone, clay and sand. The plastic rock is called plastiglomerate. Scientists first described it in 2014, on a beach in Hawaii. It was formed when fires melted plastic onto sand and stones.

ask.q: Which card was the hardest to decide? Why?
good: The cultured pearl, because the oyster and people both made it.
The plastic rock, because nature and people both made it.

flow.do: Look at the three mats and the cards on the lines between them.
flow.say: Look at the cards on the lines between the mats. Is the line between natural and made always sharp?
flow.kid: Look at the cards on the lines. Is it always easy to say who made a thing?
flow.think: Birds build nests and people build houses. Is a house as natural as a nest?

setup.caption: 1. Lay out the three court mats.

setup.caption: 2. Lawyers argue who made the thing on the card.

experiments.title: Make New Paper from Old Paper
experiments.context: In this experiment you make a new sheet of paper from old newspaper. Paper is made of plant fibres from trees. You will see the fibres, mash them and press them into a new sheet.
experiments.question: Can we make new paper from old paper? Does adding plant bits, like dried grass or petals, change the new paper?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the mashed newspaper hold together as a sheet? Which sheet will look and feel most different: plain, with dried grass, or with flower petals?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same amount of mashed paper for each sheet, and the same frame. Press each sheet the same way and dry them in the same place. Change only what you add: nothing, dried grass or petals.
results_table: Did it hold together? (yes or no)

materials.item: 4 sheets of old newspaper or used printer paper, torn into small pieces
a big bowl of warm water
a mixer jar, or a potato masher and a whisk
a small frame covered with old mosquito net or a cut piece of old net curtain, about the size of a notebook page
a tray bigger than the frame
old cotton cloths or towels and a few sheets of newspaper for drying
a handful of dried grass cut small, and a handful of marigold or other petals
a magnifying glass

experiments.safety: A grown-up uses the mixer. Do this on a floor or table covered with newspaper, because it gets wet.

schedule.what: Look at paper fibres, soak and mash the paper, and make three sheets.
Peel off the dry sheets, compare them and fill in the table.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Stick a small piece of each new sheet beside it.

flow.context: This is the first step of making new paper from old paper. First you look closely at the edge of torn paper.
flow.do: 1. Tear a strip of newspaper slowly. 2. Look at the torn edge with a magnifying glass.
flow.say: Look at the torn edge. Can you see tiny hairs sticking out? Those are plant fibres from a tree. Paper is a flat mat of tangled fibres.
flow.kid: Tear a strip of newspaper slowly. Look at the edge with a magnifier. See the tiny hairs? Those came from a tree!

ask.q: What do the tiny hairs look like?

flow.do: 1. Tear 4 sheets of newspaper into pieces the size of a stamp. 2. Soak them in warm water for at least 10 minutes. 3. A grown-up blends them with plenty of water in a mixer, in short bursts, until it looks like thin porridge. Or mash them hard with a masher and whisk.
flow.say: The water loosens the fibres from each other. Now we mash them into a soup of fibres. Paper makers call it pulp.
flow.kid: Tear the paper into tiny pieces. Soak them in warm water. Ask a grown-up to blend them. Now it is a mushy soup called pulp!
flow.parent: Use lots of water: about one big glass for every handful of paper. If you have no mixer, soak the pieces for an hour first, then mash and whisk hard for five minutes.

flow.do: 1. Pour the pulp into the tray and add water until it is about two fingers deep. Stir. 2. Slide the netted frame into the tray at an angle, then lift it flat and level. 3. Let the water drip out. 4. Flip the frame onto a cloth and press the back with a sponge or cloth to squeeze out water. 5. Lift the frame gently. The wet sheet stays on the cloth. 6. Make a second sheet with dried grass stirred into the pulp, and a third with petals.
flow.say: Lift slowly and keep the frame flat. The fibres settle on the net in a thin layer. When we squeeze out the water, they tangle and hold on to each other.
flow.kid: Dip the frame in the pulp. Lift it flat. Let it drip. Flip it onto a cloth. Press out the water. Lift the frame gently. Make three sheets: plain, grass and petals.

check.q: Why does the wet pulp hold together as a sheet?
options: The fibres tangle and grip each other as the water goes
We added glue
The net melts into it
check.why: Paper is a mat of plant fibres. As the water drains and is pressed out, the fibres tangle, and they grip each other more as they dry. No glue is needed. Picking 'glue' is a sensible guess, because things that stick usually need glue. Factories add a little starch to some paper, but the tangled fibres do most of the work.

flow.wait: Leave the sheets to dry for 1 day, or 2 days in damp weather.
flow.do: Leave the sheets on their cloths in a warm, airy place, out of the rain, until they are completely dry.
flow.say: Now we wait. Tomorrow the water will have gone into the air, and the fibres will grip even more tightly.
flow.kid: Put your sheets somewhere warm to dry. Wait until tomorrow. No peeking too early!

flow.do: 1. Peel each dry sheet off its cloth. 2. Compare the three sheets. 3. Fill in the table.
flow.say: Which sheet looks most different? Which feels roughest? Could you write on them?
flow.kid: Peel off your new paper! Compare the three sheets. Try writing your name on each one.
flow.think: Long ago, people made paper from old rags, rice straw and bark. What else around your home could you make paper from?
flow.parent: Handmade paper is thicker and bumpier than shop paper, because factory machines press it much harder and flatter. The sheets with grass or petals will show those bits. The unit on Testing materials shows how to test which paper is strongest.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: We can make new paper from old paper. What I saw: The mashed pulp dried into a sheet. The grass and petals showed up in it. Why: Paper is made of plant fibres. When we mash it, the fibres come apart. When we press and dry them, they tangle together again.

experiments.title: Salt from the Sea, Like Kashi
experiments.context: In this unit's story, Kashi finds salt on the rim of a stone hollow by the sea. In this experiment you get salt out of salty water, using only the sun.
experiments.question: Does the sun get the salt out of salty water faster than the shade does? Does it change how much salt we get?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which plate will dry first, the one in the sun or the one in the shade? Will the two plates give the same amount of salt?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use two plates that are the same. Put the same amount of the same salty water on each. Change only one thing: one plate is in the sun, one is in the shade.

materials.item: a cup of sea water, or 1 cup of tap water with 1 level teaspoon of salt stirred in until it vanishes
2 dark plates or steel thalis of the same size
a teaspoon and a magnifying glass
a sunny window sill or roof, and a shady place indoors

experiments.safety: If you collect sea water, go with a grown-up and stay out of deep water. Do not eat salt from sea water, because it may be dirty.

schedule.what: Make the salty water. Pour half a cup on each plate. Put one in the sun and one in the shade.
Check both plates. Is either dry? Write it down.
Check both plates again.
Scrape the salt from each plate. Compare the amounts. Look at the crystals with a magnifier.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw what the salt crystals looked like under the magnifier.

flow.context: This is the first step of getting salt from salty water. You make sea water, or use real sea water.
flow.do: 1. Stir 1 level teaspoon of salt into 1 cup of water until you cannot see it any more. 2. Taste one drop from your fingertip. 3. If you live near the sea, a grown-up can bring a cup of real sea water instead.
flow.say: Where did the salt go? It has not vanished. It is still there, hidden in the water, like sugar in tea. Sea water is like this. It has salt hidden in it.
flow.kid: Stir a spoon of salt into a cup of water. Where did it go? Taste one drop. It is still there, hidden!

good: It is still in the water.
It broke into tiny bits too small to see.

flow.do: 1. Pour half the cup onto each plate. 2. Put one plate in a sunny place and one in a shady place indoors. 3. Write the date and time.
flow.say: We are doing what salt makers do in salt pans. The only thing we change is the sun.
flow.kid: Pour half the water on each plate. Put one in the sun. Put one in the shade. Now wait.
flow.parent: On the coasts of Gujarat and Tamil Nadu, and in the Little Rann of Kutch, salt makers let sea water or salty underground water dry in big flat pans. In the Rann, families called Agariyas have made salt this way for generations.

flow.wait: Check both plates each day for up to 3 days.
flow.do: Each day, look at both plates. Write down when each one is completely dry.
flow.say: Which plate is drying faster? Where is the water going?
flow.kid: Check your plates every day. Which one dries first? Where is the water going?

check.q: Where does the water go as the plate dries?
options: Into the air, as tiny bits we cannot see
Into the plate
It turns into salt
check.why: The water goes into the air. Scientists say it evaporates. The sun's warmth makes it evaporate faster. The salt cannot go into the air, so it is left behind. Picking 'it turns into salt' is a very common idea. But the salt was in the water from the start. The water only leaves it behind.

flow.do: 1. When both plates are dry, look at the white crust with a magnifier. 2. Scrape the salt from each plate into a separate heap with a teaspoon. 3. Compare the two heaps.
flow.say: Look at the shapes. Salt grows in tiny cubes, like little dice. Which plate gave more salt?
flow.kid: Look at the salt with a magnifier. Do you see tiny cubes? Scrape it up. Which plate gave more?
flow.parent: Both plates should give about the same amount of salt, because each had the same amount of salt hidden in it. The sun only makes the water leave faster. Some salt sticks to the plate, so the heaps may be a little different. Slower drying in the shade often grows bigger, neater cubes.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: The sun gets salt out of water faster, but it does not make more salt. What I saw: The sunny plate dried in 1 day and the shady plate took 3 days. Both gave about the same heap of salt. Why: The salt was already hidden in the water. The sun only took the water away into the air. People do not make salt. They collect it.

experiments.title: Colours from the Kitchen
experiments.context: In this experiment you colour cotton cloth with dyes from plants in your kitchen. Then you wash the cloth to see which colours stay. Until 1856, every dye in the world came from nature.
experiments.question: Which kitchen plant gives the strongest colour to cotton cloth? Which colour stays best after washing?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Turmeric, beetroot, onion skins or tea: which will give the brightest colour? Which will wash out most?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use pieces of the same white cotton cloth, all the same size. Soak each in its dye for the same time, 30 minutes. Wash them all the same way, with the same soap. Change only the dye.
results_table: Did it stay? (well, a little, or washed out)

materials.item: 4 pieces of old white cotton cloth, each about the size of a hanky
1 teaspoon of turmeric powder
1 small beetroot, grated
the dry outer skins of 4 or 5 onions
3 tea bags or 2 spoons of tea leaves
4 steel bowls, a pan, water and a stove
a little soap

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the boiling and pours the hot dye. Turmeric and beetroot stain hands and clothes, so wear old clothes.

schedule.what: Make four dyes, soak the cloths for 30 minutes, then hang them to dry.
Wash half of each cloth, dry it, and compare the colours.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Stick a small piece of each cloth, before and after washing, beside the table.

flow.context: This is the first step of making colours from the kitchen. A grown-up boils four plant materials in water to make four dyes.
flow.do: 1. A grown-up boils each plant material in 2 cups of water for 10 minutes: the turmeric, the grated beetroot, the onion skins, and the tea. 2. Pour each coloured water into its own bowl. 3. Let it cool until it is just warm.
flow.say: The colour is hidden inside the plant. Hot water pulls it out. Before 1856, every colour on every sari in the world came from plants, animals or rocks like these.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to boil each plant in water. Watch the water change colour. The colour came out of the plant!

ask.q: Which water turned the darkest colour?

flow.do: 1. Put one wet cotton cloth into each bowl of warm dye. 2. Push it under with a spoon. 3. Leave all four for 30 minutes. 4. Squeeze them out and hang them to dry in the shade.
flow.say: Every cloth gets the same time. That way, the only difference is the dye.
flow.kid: Put one cloth in each bowl. Push it under. Wait 30 minutes. Squeeze it out. Hang it up to dry.
flow.parent: Wetting the cloth first helps the dye soak in evenly. If you like, add a spoon of salt or a little alum to the dye. Traditional dyers use alum to help some colours stay.

flow.wait: Leave the cloths to dry overnight.
flow.do: Next day, cut each cloth in half. Keep one half. Wash the other half with soap and water, rinse it, and dry it.
flow.say: Now the big test. Which colours will stay after washing?
flow.kid: Cut each cloth in half. Wash one half with soap. Keep the other half dry. Which colour will stay?

check.q: Turmeric, beetroot, onion skins and tea all came from plants. Is the dyed cloth natural, or made by people?
options: Made by people, from natural cotton and natural dyes
Natural, because everything in it came from plants
Made by people, from made materials
check.why: The cotton and the dyes all came from plants, so the materials are natural. But people changed them: they spun and wove the cotton, boiled out the dye and soaked the cloth. So the dyed cloth is made by people, from natural materials. Picking 'natural' usually means looking only at where the materials came from, not at what people did to them.

flow.do: Put the washed and unwashed halves side by side. Fill in the table.
flow.say: Which colour stayed best? Which washed out most?
flow.kid: Put the halves side by side. Which colour stayed? Which washed away?
flow.parent: Usually onion skins and tea stay quite well, and turmeric fades in sunlight and with washing. Beetroot often washes out a lot. Dyers in India learned over thousands of years which plants, and which helpers like alum, make colours last. Indigo, the famous blue, came from a plant too.
flow.think: In 1856 a teenager in England, William Perkin, made the first dye from chemicals, a bright purple. Was his dye natural or made?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: Plants can give strong colours to cotton, but some colours wash out. What I saw: The onion skin cloth stayed orange-brown after washing. The beetroot cloth went pale pink. Why: The colour was hidden inside the plants. Hot water pulled it out, and it soaked into the cotton. Some colours hold on to cotton better than others.

experiments.title: Turn Milk into Plastic
experiments.context: In this experiment you turn milk and vinegar into a kind of plastic. Long before plastic was made from oil, people made a plastic like this from milk.
experiments.question: Can we make a plastic from milk? How much vinegar makes the most milk plastic?
experiments.predict: Guess first. What will happen when we add vinegar to hot milk? Will more vinegar make more lumps?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same amount of the same milk each time, 1 cup, heated to the same warmth. Stir the same way for the same time. Change only the vinegar: 1, 2 or 4 teaspoons.
results_table: How many spoons of lumps we got

materials.item: 3 cups of milk
white vinegar, or lemon juice
a pan, a stove, a teaspoon and 3 bowls
a tea strainer or a piece of thin cotton cloth
paper towels, and a cookie cutter or a small mould if you have one

experiments.safety: A grown-up heats the milk until it is hot but not boiling, and pours it. Do not eat the milk plastic.

schedule.what: Make milk plastic with 1, 2 and 4 teaspoons of vinegar. Squeeze it and shape it.
Check the shapes. They should be dry and hard.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Keep your best milk plastic shape.

flow.context: This is the first step of turning milk into plastic. A grown-up warms the milk.
flow.do: 1. A grown-up warms 1 cup of milk in a pan until it is steaming but not boiling. 2. Pour it into a bowl. 3. Add 1 teaspoon of vinegar and stir slowly for 1 minute.
flow.say: Watch closely. Milk looks like one smooth liquid. But hidden in it is a material called casein. Vinegar makes the casein come out of the milk in lumps.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to warm the milk. Add one spoon of vinegar. Stir slowly. Watch! What do you see?

good: It split into lumps and yellowish water.

flow.do: 1. Do the same with a fresh cup of hot milk and 2 teaspoons of vinegar. 2. Then with a third cup and 4 teaspoons. 3. Pour each bowl through the strainer. 4. Count how many teaspoons of lumps each bowl gave.
flow.say: Same milk, same warmth, same stirring. Only the vinegar changes. Which bowl gives the most lumps?
flow.kid: Try again with 2 spoons of vinegar. Then 4 spoons. Strain each bowl. Count the spoons of lumps.
flow.parent: This is how paneer is made too, with lemon juice. The lumps are casein, a natural material from milk, with some milk fat. Let the lumps cool before your child touches them.

flow.do: 1. Press the cooled lumps between paper towels to squeeze out the water. 2. Knead them like dough. 3. Press them into a shape or a cookie cutter. 4. Leave the shapes to dry for 2 days.
flow.say: Now shape your plastic. As it dries, it will go hard.
flow.kid: Squeeze the lumps dry in paper towels. Knead them. Press them into a shape. Leave them to dry and harden.

check.q: Is milk plastic natural, or made by people?
options: Natural, because cows make it
Made by people, from a natural material in milk
It is not a material
check.why: The casein came from milk, a natural material. But people heated the milk, added vinegar, strained, squeezed and shaped it. So milk plastic is made by people, from a natural raw material. Picking 'natural, because cows make it' means looking only at the source. The cow made the milk, but not the plastic.

flow.wait: Leave the shapes to dry for 2 days.
flow.do: After 2 days, feel the shapes. Tap one on the table.
flow.say: About 125 years ago, factories in Germany and France made a hard plastic like this from milk. They called it Galalith, which means 'milk stone'. People made buttons, combs and fountain pens from it.
flow.kid: Feel your shape. Is it hard now? Long ago, factories made buttons from milk plastic like this!
flow.think: Today most plastic is made from oil. Why do you think factories stopped making plastic from milk?
flow.parent: Galalith was invented in 1897 and made into buttons, buckles and jewellery for decades. It soaks up water and can crack, so most factories later switched to plastics made from oil.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: We can make a plastic from milk, and more vinegar made more lumps, up to a point. What I saw: 1 teaspoon gave a few lumps. 4 teaspoons gave the most. The shapes went hard after 2 days. Why: Milk has a natural material called casein hidden in it. Vinegar made it come out in lumps. When it dried, it set hard, like plastic.

activities.title: The Journey Backwards
activities.context: In this activity you pick three things in your home and follow each one backwards, step by step, to where its material came from in nature.

materials.item: a big sheet of paper, a pencil and colours
three objects: for example a steel spoon, a cotton hanky and a plastic comb

schedule.what: Draw a backwards journey chain for three objects.

activities.record: Draw three chains of boxes with arrows, from the object back to nature.

flow.context: This is the first step of The Journey Backwards. You choose three objects to follow back to nature.
flow.do: 1. Put a steel spoon, a cotton hanky and a plastic comb on the table. 2. Pick up the spoon and ask the two detective questions.
flow.say: Two detective questions. What is it made of? And where was that, before it was this?
flow.kid: Pick up the spoon. Ask it: what are you made of? Where were you before?

ask.q: What is the spoon made of?

flow.do: For each object, draw a chain of boxes from right to left. Start with the object on the right. Keep asking 'and before that?' until you reach nature. Draw a small picture in each box.
flow.say: The shop. Before the shop? A factory. Before the factory? Keep going until you reach something nature made.
flow.kid: Draw the object in a box. Draw an arrow back. What was it before? Keep going until you reach nature.
flow.parent: Good chains. Steel spoon: shop, factory pressing steel sheets, steel made in a furnace from iron, iron ore dug from a mine in Odisha or Jharkhand, rock in the ground. Cotton hanky: shop, cloth weaving, thread spinning, cotton fluff, cotton plant in a field in Gujarat or Maharashtra, seed, soil, sun and rain. Plastic comb: shop, factory moulding plastic, plastic beads, chemicals made from petroleum, oil deep underground, tiny sea living things from millions of years ago.

check.q: Follow a plastic comb backwards. Where does it end up?
options: At a factory, because plastic is invented there
At oil deep underground, made from ancient sea life
Nowhere: plastic comes from nothing
check.why: Most plastic is made from petroleum and natural gas. These formed deep underground over millions of years, from tiny living things in ancient seas. Picking 'a factory' usually means stopping the journey too soon. The factory changes the oil, but it does not make the stuff from nothing.

flow.do: Put the three chains side by side and compare where each one ends.
flow.say: Did any chain end somewhere other than nature? Which chain was the longest?
flow.kid: Look at your three chains. Where did each one end? Did any end outside nature?
flow.think: The unit on Using the right material asks why a spoon is steel and a hanky is cotton. Can you guess?

setup.caption: 2. Draw each one's journey backwards, box by box.

activities.title: Nature or People? The Three-Heap Walk
activities.context: This is a walk where you collect small things and sort them into three heaps: living or once-living natural things, non-living natural things, and things made by people.

materials.item: a cloth bag for collecting
three dupattas or sheets of newspaper for the three heaps
a pencil and paper for a tally

activities.safety: Walk with a grown-up. Do not pick up glass, sharp things, dirty wrappers or anything an animal has left. Wash hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Collect things on a short walk, sort them into three heaps and make a tally.

activities.record: Make a tally of how many things went in each heap. Draw a bar chart of the tally.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Three-Heap Walk. You collect small things on a walk.
flow.do: Walk around a garden, a park or your lane for 10 minutes. Collect about 15 small, clean things: leaves, stones, seeds, a feather, a bottle cap, a bit of string, a twig, a shell.
flow.say: Let's collect things nature made and things people made. Only clean things, and nothing sharp.
flow.kid: Go on a walk with a grown-up. Collect 15 small, clean things. Nothing sharp!

flow.do: 1. Lay out three dupattas: LIVING OR ONCE-LIVING (natural), NEVER LIVING (natural), MADE BY PEOPLE. 2. Your child sorts each thing and says why. 3. Make a tally of each heap.
flow.say: A leaf was once part of a living tree. A stone was never alive. A bottle cap was made by people. Where does each thing go?
flow.kid: Make three heaps. Once-living natural things. Never-living natural things. Things made by people. Sort them and count.
flow.parent: Once-living: leaves, twigs, seeds, feathers, shells, flowers. Never-living: stones, sand, soil. Made by people: bottle caps, string, paper, bits of brick. A brick piece is made by people from clay. Cotton string is made by people from a once-living plant.

flow.do: Look at the tricky things together, then draw a bar chart of the tally.
flow.say: Which things were hard to sort? A bit of brick? A cotton string?
flow.kid: Which thing was hardest to sort? Why? Now draw a bar for each heap.

check.q: A piece of cotton string. Which heap?
options: Living or once-living natural
Never living natural
Made by people, from a once-living plant
check.why: The cotton came from a plant, which was alive. But people picked, spun and twisted the fibres into string. So the string is made by people, from a natural, once-living material. Picking 'once-living natural' means looking only at the source, and leaving out what people did.

activities.title: The Grandparent Time Machine
activities.context: In this activity you interview a grandparent or an older person. You find out what everyday things were made of when they were children.

materials.item: a phone or a visit
a sheet of paper with a two-column table: THEN and NOW

schedule.what: Interview a grandparent about materials then and now.

activities.record: Fill in the THEN and NOW table for six things.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Grandparent Time Machine. You get ready to interview an older person.
flow.do: Help your child write six things in the table: bucket, plate, school bag, toy, cup for tea, raincoat or umbrella.
flow.say: We are going to travel back in time, by asking questions. What were these things made of when your grandparent was your age?
flow.kid: Write six things in your table. Bucket, plate, bag, toy, tea cup, umbrella. Now let's travel back in time!

flow.do: Your child asks a grandparent the three questions for each thing. You help write down the answers.
flow.say: Ask: What was it made of when you were small? Where did that material come from? Why do you think it changed?
flow.kid: Ask your grandparent three questions. What was it made of then? Where did it come from? Why did it change?
flow.parent: Common answers. Buckets were brass, iron or aluminium. Plates were brass, bronze, steel or leaf plates called pattal. Bags were cloth or jute. Tea came in clay kulhads. Toys were wood, clay or cloth. Umbrellas were cloth on a cane or metal frame. Plastic became common in Indian homes from about the 1970s and 1980s.

flow.do: Look at the table and talk about what changed.
flow.say: Which materials changed most? Were the old ones natural or made by people? Which could go back to the Earth more easily?
flow.kid: Look at THEN and NOW. Which things changed most? Which could go back to the Earth?
flow.think: Which old material would you bring back, and why?

activities.title: The Material Map of India
activities.context: In this activity you make a map of India that shows where some of our materials come from: cotton, silk, jute, rubber, coir, iron, salt and more.

materials.item: a printed outline map of India
colours, and small samples if you have them: cotton wool, a jute string, a rubber band, a pinch of salt, a coir strand, a piece of foil
glue

schedule.what: Mark and stick materials on a map of India.

activities.record: A labelled map with at least 8 materials marked where they come from.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Material Map of India. You find out that materials come from real places.
flow.do: Lay out the map and the samples. Pick up the cotton wool.
flow.say: Every material comes from a real place, where real people grow it, dig it or collect it. Let's put our materials on the map.
flow.kid: Every material comes from a real place. Let's find where on the map!

flow.do: Mark each material on the map, with a small drawing or a stuck-on sample. Use the parent note for places.
flow.say: Cotton grows a lot in Gujarat and Maharashtra. Where shall we stick it?
flow.kid: Stick each material on its place on the map. Draw a little picture next to it.
flow.parent: Cotton: Gujarat, Maharashtra and Telangana. Jute: West Bengal. Silk: Karnataka, and many other states. Muga, a golden silk, comes only from Assam. Rubber: Kerala, and also Tripura. Coir from coconut husks: Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Tea: Assam and West Bengal. Iron ore: Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Karnataka. Bauxite for aluminium: Odisha. Salt: Gujarat, especially the Little Rann of Kutch, and Tamil Nadu. Marble: Makrana in Rajasthan, the marble of the Taj Mahal. Lac: Jharkhand.

ask.q: Which part of India gives the most materials on your map?
good: The east, because of iron ore and jute.
The coasts, because of salt and coir.

flow.do: Pick one material and talk about the people who work with it there.
flow.say: Who do you think does the work in each of these places? Farmers, miners, salt makers, weavers?
flow.kid: Choose one place on your map. Who works there? What is their day like?

check.q: Salt in Gujarat's Little Rann of Kutch is made by…
options: Machines that make salt from nothing
Families who let salty water dry in the sun in big pans
Digging salt out of iron mines
check.why: In the Little Rann of Kutch, families called Agariyas pump up salty underground water into big flat pans. The sun dries the water away, and the salt is left. They collect it by hand. Picking 'machines that make salt' usually means thinking made things are made from nothing. Salt is collected, not made.
