activities.title: Spin a Thread
activities.context: In this activity you turn fluffy cotton into a thread by twisting it, the first step in making cloth. You make a simple spindle from a pencil and a disc.

materials.item: a ball of cotton wool, the kind from a medical shop
a pencil, and a disc of thick cardboard or an old CD with a hole for the pencil
a ruler
a takli, a small Indian hand spindle, if you have one

activities.safety: No special safety needs. Keep the spindle away from faces when it spins.

schedule.what: Pull and twist cotton into thread with your fingers, then with a spindle.

activities.record: Measure your longest thread with a ruler. Tape it into your notebook.

flow.context: This is the first step of Spin a Thread. You first twist cotton into thread with just your fingers.
flow.do: 1. Pull a little cotton wool out into a thin, fluffy strip. 2. Pull gently on the strip. 3. Now twist one end between your fingers while you pull slowly.
flow.say: Pull without twisting, and the cotton just comes apart. Now twist while you pull. The tiny fibres wrap around each other and grip.
flow.kid: Pull a little cotton out. Does it come apart? Now twist while you pull. Feel it become a thread!

ask.q: What changed when you started twisting?

flow.do: 1. Push the pencil through the middle of the disc to make a spindle. 2. Tie a short thread to the pencil and hook the cotton onto it. 3. Spin the pencil like a top while you pull the cotton out slowly. 4. Wind the new thread around the pencil.
flow.say: This is how people spun thread for thousands of years. The disc keeps the spindle turning. In 1930 Gandhi asked Indians to spin their own thread, to make khadi cloth.
flow.kid: Make a spindle from a pencil and a disc. Spin it like a top. Pull the cotton slowly. Wind up your thread.
flow.parent: This is hard at first, so praise any thread at all. Short, lumpy thread is normal. Spinners practise for years to make fine, even thread.

check.q: Is your cotton thread natural, or made by people?
options: Natural, because cotton grows on plants
Made by people, from a natural plant fibre
Made by people, from oil
check.why: Cotton fluff grows on the cotton plant, so the material is natural. But you twisted it into a thread, so the thread is made by people. Picking 'from oil' mixes cotton up with synthetic fibres like nylon and polyester, which are made from petroleum.

flow.do: Measure your longest thread with a ruler. Tape it into the notebook.
flow.say: How long is your thread? One sari needs hundreds of metres of thread.
flow.kid: Measure your thread with a ruler. Tape it in your notebook.
flow.think: The fine Dhaka muslin of old Bengal was spun by hand, so thin it could pass through a ring. How many hours do you think it took?

activities.title: Same Beads, Different Things
activities.context: This activity uses beads as pretend atoms. You build different 'materials' from the same three kinds of bead, to see how a few atoms make everything.

materials.item: beads, buttons or small sweets in three colours: black for carbon, white for hydrogen, red for oxygen
toothpicks or pipe cleaners to join them

activities.safety: Keep small beads away from babies and toddlers, who might swallow them.

schedule.what: Build pretend materials from three kinds of bead.

activities.record: Draw two of your bead models and label the colours.

flow.context: This is the first step of Same Beads, Different Things. You use beads as pretend atoms.
flow.do: Sort the beads into three colours. Say what each colour stands for: black is carbon, white is hydrogen, red is oxygen.
flow.say: Everything is made of tiny atoms. These beads are pretend atoms. Wood, cotton, sugar and plastic are made mostly from just these three kinds.
flow.kid: These beads are pretend atoms. Black is carbon. White is hydrogen. Red is oxygen.

flow.do: 1. Build a long chain of black beads, with two white beads on each black one. This stands for plastic, like a plastic bag. 2. Build little rings of black beads with red and white beads on them, joined in a chain. This stands for cellulose, the stuff of cotton and wood. 3. Build one red bead with two white beads. This is water.
flow.say: Look. A plastic bag and a cotton hanky are made of almost the same atoms. Only the pattern is different.
flow.kid: Build a long chain: one black, two whites, again and again. That is like plastic! Now build cotton with rings.

flow.do: Mix all the beads up again and talk.
flow.say: When people make a material, they do not make new beads. They only join them in new patterns.
flow.kid: Break your models up. Could you build something new? People never make new atoms. They make new patterns.

check.q: A wooden spoon and a plastic spoon are both made mostly of…
options: Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms, in different patterns
Completely different atoms that have nothing in common
Wood atoms and plastic atoms
check.why: Wood and plastic are both made mostly of carbon and hydrogen, and wood has a lot of oxygen too. They are different because the atoms are joined in different patterns. Picking 'wood atoms and plastic atoms' is a very common idea. But there is no such thing as a wood atom. Wood is made of ordinary atoms, like everything else.

activities.title: We Are Stardust: Act It Out
activities.context: This is a short play where children act as atoms. They are made in a star, blown into space when it dies, and become a new planet, and then a steel spoon.

materials.item: a torch for the star, and some open space
a steel spoon

activities.safety: Move slowly and clear the space of anything breakable.

schedule.what: Act out the journey of an atom from a star to a spoon.

activities.record: Draw a comic strip in four boxes: star, explosion, Earth, spoon.

flow.context: This is the first step of We Are Stardust, a play about where atoms come from.
flow.do: 1. The grown-up holds the torch. That is a big star. 2. The children crouch close together around it. They are small atoms, hydrogen, squeezed in the star's hot middle.
flow.say: You are tiny hydrogen atoms inside a giant star. It is very hot and very squeezed. Hold hands in twos and fours. Now you have joined into bigger atoms: carbon, oxygen and iron!
flow.kid: You are a tiny atom inside a star. It is hot and squeezed! Hold hands. Now you are a bigger atom, like iron.

flow.do: 1. The grown-up switches the torch off and on fast, and says 'BOOM!' 2. The children spin slowly out across the room. That is the star exploding. 3. Then they drift together into a ball in one corner. That is a new planet forming: the Earth.
flow.say: The old star dies and explodes. You are flung into space as dust. After a very long time, the dust gathers into a new Sun and new planets. You are inside the Earth now, as iron in a rock.
flow.kid: BOOM! The star explodes. Spin slowly into space. Now drift together. You are part of the new Earth!

check.q: Where was the iron in a steel spoon made, long ago?
options: In the spoon factory
Inside a star
In the mine
check.why: Iron atoms were made inside stars, long before the Earth formed. The iron sat in rocks in the ground. People dug up the ore and melted out the iron in a furnace. The factory made the spoon, and the mine gave the ore. But only a star can make the iron atoms. Picking 'the mine' stops the journey too early.

flow.do: 1. The grown-up 'digs up' one child, the iron atom, and leads them to the table. 2. The child holds up the steel spoon.
flow.say: Miners dug you out. A furnace melted you. A factory pressed you into a spoon. And here you are, at our dinner table. A little piece of a star.
flow.kid: A miner digs you up. A furnace melts you. Now you are a spoon! A little piece of a star.
flow.think: Scientists still argue about where gold atoms were made. Was it exploding stars, or two dead stars crashing together?

projects.title: From Soil to Diya
projects.context: In this 5-day project you make a small diya from soil you dig yourself. You find the clay in it, shape it and dry it. You weigh it before and after drying. Then you compare it with a diya baked in a kiln.

materials.item: 2 big cups of soil from a garden, a field or a riverbank, not from a pot with fertiliser
a bucket of water, a tall clear bottle or jar, and an old cloth for straining
a kitchen scale
a bought clay diya, baked in a kiln, to compare

projects.safety: Dig only where a grown-up says you may. Wear old clothes. Wash hands after handling soil. A grown-up lights any diya, and never leaves a lit diya alone.

schedule.what: Dig soil, shake it in water in a bottle, and leave it to settle into layers.
Pour off the water, scoop out the fine clay, and strain and dry it to dough.
Knead the clay, shape a diya and weigh it wet.
Check that it is drying slowly in the shade.
Weigh the dry diya. Compare it with a kiln-baked diya. Drip water on both.

projects.record: Draw the layers in the jar. Write the wet and dry weights of your diya. Write what happened when water dripped on each diya.

flow.context: This is the first step of From Soil to Diya. You find the clay hidden in ordinary soil by letting it settle in water.
flow.do: 1. Dig 2 cups of soil. Pick out stones, roots and leaves. 2. Put half the soil into a tall clear bottle. Fill it nearly to the top with water. 3. Close it and shake hard for one minute. 4. Leave it still overnight. 5. Put the rest of the soil in a bucket of water, stir and leave it too.
flow.say: Soil is a mix of many things. Water will sort it for us. The heavy bits sink first. The finest bits, the clay, sink last.
flow.kid: Dig some soil. Pick out stones and roots. Shake it in a bottle of water. Leave it still until tomorrow.

flow.do: 1. Look at the bottle. Draw the layers you see. 2. In the bucket, gently pour off the clear water on top. 3. Scoop out the smooth top layer of mud, the clay. 4. Wrap it in a cloth and hang it up, or leave it on newspaper, until it is like soft dough.
flow.say: See the layers? Stones and sand at the bottom, then silt, then the smooth clay on top. Clay grains are the tiniest of all.
flow.kid: Look at the layers in your bottle! Draw them. Scoop the smooth top mud from the bucket. That is clay!

check.q: In the bottle, why is the clay on the top?
options: Clay grains are the tiniest, so they sink last
Clay floats like oil
Someone poured it in last
check.why: Big, heavy grains like sand sink fast. The tiny grains of clay sink very slowly, so they settle last, on top. Picking 'clay floats' is a fair guess. But clay does sink if you wait long enough. It is just slow.

flow.parent: Some soils have very little clay. If yours has hardly any, buy a small packet of potter's clay and mix it in. Riverbank and field soil often has plenty.

flow.do: 1. Knead the clay until it is smooth and does not crack when bent. 2. Roll a ball the size of a lemon. 3. Press your thumb in the middle and pinch the sides up into a cup. 4. Pinch one side into a spout for a wick. 5. Weigh the wet diya on the kitchen scale and write the number.
flow.say: Potters in India have shaped diyas like this for thousands of years. At Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, people baked clay pots more than 4,000 years ago.
flow.kid: Knead the clay smooth. Roll a ball. Push your thumb in. Pinch up the sides. Make a spout. Weigh it!
flow.parent: If it cracks, it is too dry, so wet your fingers. If it sags, it is too wet, so let it firm up for an hour.

flow.wait: Leave the diya to dry slowly in the shade for 2 days.
flow.do: Put the diya in a shady, airy place. Drying too fast in the sun can crack it.
flow.say: Now we wait. The water inside will slowly go into the air.
flow.kid: Put your diya in the shade to dry. Not in hot sun, or it might crack.

flow.do: 1. Weigh the dry diya and write the number. 2. Work out how much water left it. 3. Put your diya and the bought diya side by side. 4. Drip a few drops of water on the edge of each and watch for a minute.
flow.say: The bought diya was baked in a kiln, a very hot oven. Our diya was only dried in the air. What happens when water touches each one?
flow.kid: Weigh your dry diya. Is it lighter? Drip water on your diya and on a bought one. What happens?

chart.title: Made-up example: our diya, wet and dry

check.q: Water dripped on our air-dried diya makes it go soft. The kiln-baked diya stays hard. Why?
options: Baking in a kiln changes clay for ever, into hard pottery
The bought diya has paint on it
Our clay was the wrong colour
check.why: Air-drying only takes the water out, so wet clay can soften again. A kiln heats clay so much that its tiny grains change and fuse together. Then it can never turn back into soft clay. That is why pots and bricks are baked. Picking 'paint' is a sensible guess, but most diyas are not painted where water touched them.

challenges.title: The Leaf Plate Picnic
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You make a plate and a bowl for a picnic using only natural materials, with nothing made by people.
challenges.problem: Make one plate and one small bowl for a picnic, using only natural materials you can find. They must hold a roti and a spoon of dal without leaking.
constraints: You can only use natural materials: leaves, twigs, grass, and so on.
No glue, tape, plastic, staples or thread from a shop.
It must hold a roti and one spoon of dal for 5 minutes.
materials: big leaves: banana, sal, or any big, soft, clean leaf a grown-up says is safe
thin twigs or broom sticks, called seenk, for pins
a pair of scissors for the grown-up
general: Overlap several leaves in a circle and pin them with thin twig slivers. This is how pattals, leaf plates, are made in India.
Fold a leaf into a cone or a cup and pin the fold. This is how a dona, a leaf bowl, is made.
Use a single big banana leaf as a plate, as is done at many South Indian meals.
creative: Weave long grass or coconut leaf strips into a small mat, then line it with a leaf.
Use half a coconut shell as a bowl. It is natural, strong and lasts years.
Press leaves together while damp and let them dry in a stack, so they hold their shape.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own natural plate or bowl. Test it with a roti and a spoon of dal. Does it leak?

flow.context: This is the first step of the Leaf Plate Picnic challenge. You look at how leaf plates are made.
flow.do: 1. Collect big clean leaves and thin twigs with a grown-up. 2. Look at a bought pattal or a picture of one, if you can.
flow.say: For thousands of years, people in India ate from leaves. Leaf plates are still sold in markets. After the meal, cows can eat them or they rot into soil.
flow.kid: Collect big leaves and thin twigs with a grown-up. People in India have eaten from leaves for thousands of years!

flow.do: Before building, draw two ideas: one for the plate and one for the bowl.
flow.say: Engineers draw before they build. How will you stop the dal leaking out?
flow.kid: Draw your plate and bowl first. How will you stop the dal from leaking?

flow.do: 1. Build the plate and bowl. 2. Put a roti on the plate and a spoon of dal in the bowl. 3. Wait 5 minutes and check for leaks.
flow.say: Build it, then test it. If it leaks, what will you change?
flow.kid: Build your plate and bowl. Put in a roti and a spoon of dal. Wait 5 minutes. Any leaks?
flow.parent: Leaves with a waxy top side, like banana leaves, hold liquid best. Twig pins work best when snapped short and sharp. A grown-up can trim the twigs with scissors.

check.q: After the picnic, what happens to a leaf plate thrown on the soil?
options: It decomposes into soil in weeks or months
It stays for hundreds of years
It melts in the sun
check.why: Leaves are made by living plants. Tiny living things in the soil, like bacteria and fungi, break them down into soil. Scientists say they decompose. Picking 'stays for hundreds of years' mixes leaves up with some plastics, which tiny living things can hardly break down.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas together. Then improve your design.
flow.say: Here is how people usually do it, and some creative ideas. Can you make yours better?
flow.kid: Look at the usual ways and some new ideas. Can you make your plate even better?
flow.think: Why do you think so many people switched from leaf plates to plastic and paper plates? Was it a good swap?

challenges.title: Swap the Plastic
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You choose one plastic thing in your home and design a replacement made from a natural material, or a material that lasts for many years.
challenges.problem: Choose one plastic thing your family throws away often, like a straw, a carry bag or a cling film wrap. Design something to replace it, made from a natural material or one that lasts for years.
constraints: It must do the same job as well.
It must not cost much more.
You must say where its material comes from, and what happens to it when it is old.
materials: things from home to try: cloth, jute, steel, bamboo, paper, leaves, beeswax, old saris
general: A cloth or jute bag in place of plastic carry bags.
A steel or bamboo straw, or a papaya stalk, in place of a plastic straw.
A steel tiffin box in place of cling film.
creative: Wax wraps: cotton cloth soaked in melted beeswax, to cover bowls.
A bag sewn from an old sari or kurta.
A kulhad, a clay cup, which can go back to the soil.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own swap. Draw it, label its materials, and write where each material comes from.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Swap the Plastic challenge. You choose a plastic thing your family throws away.
flow.do: Look in the kitchen dustbin or recycling bag together. List the plastic things you find.
flow.say: Which plastic things do we throw away most? Pick one to swap.
flow.kid: Look in the dustbin with a grown-up. Which plastic things do we throw away? Pick one.

flow.do: 1. Draw a replacement. 2. Label each material. 3. Write where each material comes from and what happens to it when it gets old.
flow.say: What job does the plastic thing do? What could do the same job, and come from nature or last for years?
flow.kid: Draw your new design. Label its materials. Where does each one come from?

check.q: Which swap can go back into the soil when it is old?
options: A kulhad, a clay cup that was not glazed
A plastic cup
A steel cup
check.why: A plain clay kulhad is baked earth. When it breaks, its pieces slowly crumble back into the soil. A steel cup lasts for many years and can be melted and remade, which is also good. A plastic cup is usually used once and lasts a very long time. Picking 'steel' is not a bad choice, because steel lasts long. But it does not go back into soil.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and creative ideas. Then try making a simple version of your swap, if you can.
flow.say: Here are some usual swaps and some creative ones. Could your family really use yours?
flow.kid: Look at the usual swaps and some new ideas. Try making yours. Will your family use it?
flow.parent: The unit on Using the right material goes deeper into choosing a material for a job.
flow.think: Is the best swap the one that is most natural, the one that lasts longest, or the one people will really use?

items.p: A steel tumbler. Which word names its material?
items.why: Steel is the stuff it is made of, so it is the material. 'Tumbler' is the object's name. Picking 'tumbler' usually means mixing up the object and the material. Ask: if you broke it into tiny bits, what would the bits be?

items.p: Sort these. Natural, or made by people?
items.why: Nature made the pebble, the mango, the feather and the rain. People made the bangle, brick, bucket and spoon, from natural materials.

items.p: Match each material to its source.
items.why: Every material comes from somewhere in nature: a plant, an animal, the ground or the sea.

items.p: Where does most plastic come from?
opts: From petroleum, an oil deep underground
From nothing: it is invented in factories
items.why: Most plastic is made from petroleum and natural gas, which formed from ancient sea life. Picking 'from nothing' usually means stopping the journey at the factory. Factories change materials. They never make stuff from nothing.

items.p: A natural material before people change it is called a ____ material.
items.why: Raw materials are the starting stuff, like cotton fluff, clay or iron ore.

items.p: A natural thing can be living or non-living.
items.why: True. A tree and a bird are natural and living. A rock and water are natural and non-living.

items.p: A wooden chair. Which is right?
opts: It is natural, because wood is natural
It is made by people, from a natural material
It is made by people, from a made material
It is not made of anything
items.why: Wood is a natural material, but a carpenter cut and joined it into a chair. So the chair is made by people from a natural material. Picking 'natural' means looking only at the material, not at what people did with it.

items.p: Match each raw material to what people do to it.
pairs: melt it in a furnace into glass
dry it in the sun to get salt
items.why: People change raw materials in different ways: spinning, baking, melting and drying.

items.p: Which of these comes from an animal?
items.why: Silk comes from the cocoon of a silkworm, a moth's caterpillar. Jute, coir and rubber all come from plants. Picking 'rubber' is a common mix-up, because rubber feels a bit like skin. It comes from the milky sap of a tree.

items.p: Salt comes mostly from the ____.
items.why: Sea water has salt hidden in it. In salt pans, the sun dries the water away and the salt is left.
items.context: In this unit's story, Kashi finds white salt on the rim of a stone hollow by the sea.

items.p: In the salt experiment, where did the salt come from?
opts: It was hidden in the water all along
items.why: The salt was dissolved in the water from the start. The sun only took the water away into the air. Picking 'the sun made it' is a very common idea. The sun helps us collect salt, but it does not make it.
items.context: In the salt experiment, you put the same salty water on two plates. One plate went in the sun and one in the shade. You waited for each to dry.

items.p: Paper is made from plant fibres.
items.why: True. Paper is a flat mat of tangled fibres, usually from trees. You can see them at a torn edge with a magnifier.
items.context: In the paper experiment, you looked at the torn edge of newspaper and then made new paper from old paper.

items.p: Choose one object in your home. Write its journey backwards, from the shop to nature, in at least three steps.
items.a: For example: my cotton hanky. Before the shop, it was woven from thread in a mill. Before that, the thread was spun from cotton fluff. Before that, the cotton grew on a plant in a field.
items.why: Any journey that ends in nature, with at least three correct steps, is right.

items.p: Is a cotton kurta natural, or made by people? Explain your answer.
items.a: It is made by people, from a natural material. The cotton grew on a plant, but people spun it, wove it and stitched it.
items.why: A good answer names both the natural material and what people did to it.

items.p: Draw one thing that nature made and one thing that people made. Label what each is made of.
items.a: For example: a leaf, made of plant material, and a steel spoon, made of metal from iron ore.
items.why: Any correct pair with labels is right.
items.art: Two empty boxes labelled with a tree symbol and a hand symbol.

items.p: Put the journey of a cotton kurta in order, from nature to you.
items.why: Cotton grows on a plant. The fluff is picked, spun into thread, woven into cloth and stitched by a tailor.

items.p: Put the journey of a steel spoon in order, from nature to you.
items.why: The iron is in ore in the ground. Miners dig it out. A furnace melts out the iron, which becomes steel. A factory shapes the spoon.

items.p: Paper wasps make their nests out of paper. What do they make it from?
items.why: Paper wasps chew wood and mix it with their spit. It dries as paper. In 1719 René Réaumur watched them and said people could make paper from wood too. Picking 'old newspapers' is a fun guess, but wasps were making paper long before people had newspapers.

items.p: Is the milk plastic you made natural, or made by people?
opts: Natural, because it came from a cow
Made by people, from a natural material in milk
items.why: Casein came from milk, a natural material. But you heated it, added vinegar, strained and shaped it. So it is made by people. Picking 'from oil' mixes it up with most modern plastics, which are made from petroleum.
items.context: In the milk plastic experiment, you added vinegar to hot milk, strained out the lumps and shaped them. They dried hard.

items.p: Look at the chart from the salt experiment. Why did the sunny plate dry first?
opts: The sun's warmth made the water go into the air faster
The sunny plate had less water
The shady plate was colder, so salt stopped the water leaving
items.why: Both plates had the same water. The only change was the sun. Warmth makes water evaporate, or go into the air, faster. Picking 'less water' would make the test unfair, and we kept the water the same.
items.context: In the salt experiment, you put the same salty water on two plates. One plate went in the sun and one in the shade. You waited for each to dry.

chart.title: Days until each plate was dry

items.p: Sort these by their source.
items.why: Jute and coir are plant fibres. Silk, wool and lac come from animals. Glass comes from sand, clay from the ground, and salt from the sea.

items.p: Factory indigo and plant indigo are…
opts: The very same substance, made two ways
items.why: Chemists showed that factory indigo is exactly the same substance as plant indigo. It is made by people, but it is not different. Picking 'completely different' usually means thinking made things can never be the same as natural things.
items.context: Indigo is a blue dye. For thousands of years it came from the leaves of the indigo plant. Since 1897 it has also been made in factories.

items.p: Before 1856, every dye in the world came from plants, animals or rocks.
items.why: True. In 1856 William Perkin made the first dye from chemicals, a purple called mauve. Before that, colours came from nature, like turmeric, indigo and lac.

items.p: In the colour experiment, why did we soak every cloth for the same time?
opts: So the only difference was the dye
So the cloths would dry faster
items.why: In a fair test you change only one thing. Here that was the dye. If one cloth soaked longer, it might be darker for that reason. Picking 'dry faster' is a guess about time, but soaking time is about fairness. The unit on Testing materials has much more about fair tests.
items.context: In the colour experiment, you dyed four cotton cloths with turmeric, beetroot, onion skins and tea.

items.p: A diya dried in the air goes soft when water drips on it. A kiln-baked diya stays hard. Why?
opts: A kiln heats clay so much that it changes for ever
Air-dried clay is a different material
Kiln diyas are made of plastic
items.why: A kiln heats clay until its tiny grains change and fuse. Then it cannot turn back into soft clay. Air drying only removes water. Picking 'a different material' is close, but both started as the same clay. The kiln changed it.
items.context: In the From Soil to Diya project, you made a diya from soil and dried it in the air. Then you compared it with a bought diya that was baked in a kiln.

items.p: In the bottle of shaken soil and water, the finest grains settled on top. These grains are called ____.
items.why: Clay grains are the tiniest, so they sink slowest and settle last, on top.

items.p: Match each made material to the natural material it was made from.
items.why: Every made material starts as a natural one.

items.p: Kashi first thought the government made salt in a factory. What did she find out at the stone hollow?
items.a: She found out that nobody makes salt. It is hidden in sea water. The sun takes the water into the air, and the salt is left behind. People only collect it.
items.why: A good answer says the salt was already in the sea, and the sun left it behind.
items.context: In this unit's story, Kashi lives by the sea in Gujarat in 1930. Salt is taxed, and only the government may collect it.

items.p: Name three people whose work is hidden inside a cotton kurta. Say what each one did.
items.a: A farmer grew the cotton. A spinner spun the thread. A weaver wove the cloth. A tailor stitched it.
items.why: Any three correct workers with their jobs are right.

items.p: Draw the layers you saw in the bottle of shaken soil and water. Label them.
items.a: Pebbles and sand at the bottom, then silt, then smooth clay, then clear water at the top.
items.why: Heavier grains sink first, so they are at the bottom. The finest grains, clay, are on top.

items.p: A cultured pearl is grown by an oyster on a farm, after people put a tiny bead inside it. Who made it?
items.why: The oyster made every layer of pearl, but people started it and looked after the oyster. So both played a part. Picking only one leaves out the other's part. This shows the line between natural and made is not always sharp.

items.p: A wooden spoon and a plastic spoon are both made mostly of which atoms?
items.why: Wood and plastic are both built mostly from carbon and hydrogen, and wood has lots of oxygen too. Only the patterns differ. Picking 'wood atoms and plastic atoms' is very common. But no such atoms exist. Everything is made of the same 90 or so kinds.

items.p: When people make a new material, they make new atoms.
items.why: False. People only join existing atoms in new patterns. New atoms are made only in places like the middle of stars.

items.p: Where were the iron atoms in a steel kadhai made?
opts: Inside stars, long before the Earth formed
items.why: Iron atoms were made inside stars. The Earth formed from dust that held them. Picking 'the furnace' or 'the mine' stops the journey too soon. The furnace melts iron out of ore, and the mine digs up the ore, but neither makes the atoms.

items.p: Scientists still argue about where most gold atoms were made. Which is one of the main ideas?
opts: In crashes between two dead stars called neutron stars
items.why: In 2017 telescopes saw two neutron stars crash, throwing out heavy atoms. Many scientists think crashes like this make much of the gold. Others think rare exploding stars also make some. Picking 'gold mines' confuses where we find gold with where it was made.

items.p: Is plastic completely unnatural?
opts: Yes, it has nothing to do with nature
It is made by people, but from petroleum, which formed from ancient living things
items.why: Plastic is made by people, through chemistry. But its raw material, petroleum, formed from tiny sea living things over millions of years. Picking 'nothing to do with nature' means stopping the journey at the factory.

items.p: A diamond grown in a laboratory is…
opts: A real diamond, made by people
Glass pretending to be a diamond
items.why: A lab diamond is pure carbon in the same pattern as a mined diamond. It is real diamond, made by people. Picking 'glass' confuses it with a fake. A fake is a different material that only looks like diamond.

items.p: In 2017, scientists counted all the plastic waste ever made. About ____ parts in every 100 had been recycled.
items.why: Geyer, Jambeck and Law found that only about 9 out of every 100 parts had been recycled. Most was buried or ended up on land and in the sea.

items.p: By about 2020, everything people have made weighed about as much as all the living things on Earth.
items.why: True. Scientists in Israel, led by Emily Elhacham and Ron Milo, worked this out in 2020. In 1900, made things weighed only about 3 parts for every 100 parts of living things.
items.context: This question is about how much stuff people have made: buildings, roads, machines and plastic.

items.p: A new kind of rock was found on a beach in Hawaii. What is it made of?
opts: Melted plastic mixed with sand and stones
items.why: Scientists described it in 2014 and called it plastiglomerate. Fires on the beach melted plastic onto sand, shells and stones. Picking 'frozen sea water' is a fun guess, but Hawaii's beaches are warm. The rock shows that made materials are now mixing into the Earth itself.

items.p: The oldest cotton threads ever found were found…
opts: At Mehrgarh, in South Asia, about 8,000 years old
In a factory in England, 200 years ago
items.why: Cotton threads wound around a copper bead were found at Mehrgarh, in present-day Pakistan. They are about 8,000 years old. Picking England is a common idea, because England's mills made huge amounts of cloth in the 1800s. But cotton cloth began in South Asia thousands of years earlier.

items.p: Kashi gave her salt away and did not sell it. Who do you think should own the salt in the sea? Give a reason.
items.a: Any thoughtful answer with a reason. For example: everyone, because nobody made it. Or: the people who live by the sea and do the work of collecting it.
items.why: There is no single right answer. What counts is a clear reason.
items.context: In this unit's story, Kashi finds that nobody makes salt. The sea holds it and the sun leaves it behind. In 1930 the law said only the British government could collect it.

items.p: Birds build nests and people build houses. Is a house natural or made by people? Is a nest? Explain your thinking.
items.a: A good answer might say: a nest is natural, because a bird built it from natural things. A house is made by people. But people are animals too, so perhaps a house is natural in a way. It depends on what we mean by 'natural'.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Good answers give reasons for both sides.

items.p: Factory indigo was cheaper, so plant indigo stopped being grown. Was that good or bad for the farmers? Give one reason for each side.
items.a: Good: farmers were no longer forced to grow indigo, and could grow food. Bad: people who earned money making plant indigo lost their work.
items.why: A balanced answer gives a reason on each side.
items.context: Indigo is a blue dye. For thousands of years it came from the indigo plant. In the 1800s, many farmers in Bengal and Bihar were forced to grow it. In 1897 factory indigo was first sold.

items.p: Plan a test to find out whether a 'natural' cloth or a 'made' cloth dries faster. Say what you would change and what you would keep the same.
items.a: Take a cotton cloth and a polyester cloth of the same size. Wet them with the same amount of water. Hang them in the same place. Change only the cloth. Check every 10 minutes which is dry.
items.why: A good test changes only one thing, the cloth, and keeps everything else the same. The unit on Testing materials goes further with fair tests.

quiz.p: A tumbler can be made of steel, glass or plastic. Steel, glass and plastic are…
quiz.why: They are materials, the stuff objects are made of. Picking 'objects' mixes up the thing and its stuff.
Wool is the coat of a sheep, cut and spun. Picking 'a cotton plant' mixes up two soft fibres. Cotton grows on plants, wool on animals.
Glass is made by melting sand with soda ash and limestone in a furnace. Picking 'ice' is a natural guess, because glass and ice both look clear. But ice melts at room heat and glass does not.
Nature made the neem tree. People made the others from natural materials. Picking 'a brick' means remembering that clay is natural, but forgetting that people baked it.

quiz.p: A potted tulsi plant. Which is right?
opts: The plant is natural and the pot is made by people
quiz.why: The tulsi grew by itself from a seed, so it is natural. The pot was made by people. Picking 'both made by people' usually means thinking that whatever people look after is made by them.

quiz.p: How do people get glass from sand?
quiz.why: Sand must be melted at a very high heat in a furnace. Picking 'dry it in the sun' mixes glass up with salt. The sun is far too cool to melt sand.

quiz.p: What is the raw material for a matka?
quiz.why: A matka is made from clay, shaped and baked in a kiln. Picking 'glass' mixes it up with a bottle.

quiz.p: In the salt experiment, which plate gave more salt?
opts: About the same, because both had the same salt hidden in them
The sunny plate, because the sun makes salt
The shady plate, because shade makes salt
quiz.why: The salt was in the water from the start. The sun only made the water leave faster. Picking 'the sun makes salt' is the most common idea. Salt is collected, not made.
quiz.context: In the salt experiment, you put the same salty water on two plates. One plate went in the sun and one in the shade. You waited for each to dry.

quiz.p: Why did the wet paper pulp hold together as a sheet?
opts: The plant fibres tangled and gripped each other
quiz.why: Paper is a mat of tangled plant fibres. As the water left, the fibres tangled and gripped. Picking 'water is a glue' is a fair guess, but wet paper falls apart. It is the drying fibres that hold.
quiz.context: In the paper experiment, you mashed old newspaper into pulp, lifted it on a netted frame and let it dry.

quiz.p: Which animal makes a material that people use for bangles and varnish?
quiz.why: Lac insects on trees make a resin. People scrape it off for lac bangles, varnish and sealing wax. Picking 'the cow' usually means thinking of milk, which makes paneer and milk plastic, not lac.

opts: The same substance as plant indigo
A different colour from plant indigo
quiz.why: Chemists showed they are exactly the same substance. Picking 'a different colour' means thinking made copies can never match nature.

quiz.p: Everything, natural or made, is built from…
opts: Thousands of kinds of atom, one for each material
quiz.why: About 90 kinds of atom are found in nature. They join in different patterns to build everything. Picking 'one for each material' is a very common idea. But there is no 'wood atom' or 'plastic atom'.

quiz.p: Where were the carbon atoms in your pencil made?
quiz.why: Carbon atoms were made in stars before the Earth formed. Picking 'in the tree' is close: trees take carbon from the air to build wood. But they collect carbon atoms. They do not make them.

quiz.p: Do scientists fully agree on where gold atoms were made?
opts: No. Many think neutron star crashes, others think exploding stars too
Yes, gold is made in mines
Yes, gold is made in volcanoes
quiz.why: It is still being worked out. Picking 'in mines' confuses where we find gold with where its atoms were made.

quiz.p: Who grows the cotton for a kurta?
quiz.why: A farmer grows the cotton. The tailor stitches the kurta at the end of the journey. Picking 'a tailor' means starting the journey at the shop instead of the field.

applications: Farmers grow cotton, jute and silk for cloth, and rubber trees for tyres and chappals.
Miners dig iron ore, bauxite and coal, and furnaces turn ore into iron, steel and aluminium.
Salt makers in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu dry sea water and salty ground water in the sun.
Potters and brick makers dig clay and bake it in kilns.
Glass makers in Firozabad melt sand into bangles and bottles.
Paper mills and handmade paper makers turn wood, bamboo, rags and old paper into new paper.
Recyclers, kabadiwalas and waste pickers collect old paper, metal and plastic so they can be made into new things.
Chemists invent synthetic materials, like nylon and polyester, often to copy or replace natural ones.
Dyers use plants like indigo, turmeric and madder, and also factory dyes, to colour cloth.
Scientists who study meteorites and starlight work out where the atoms in our materials were made.
Engineers are testing ways to make bricks and oxygen from Moon dust for future Moon bases.
Archaeologists study old materials, like the cotton at Mehrgarh, to learn how people lived thousands of years ago.

open_questions.q: Where were most gold atoms made: in exploding stars, or in crashes of dead stars?
open_questions.why_open: Telescopes saw one neutron star crash in 2017, but it is not clear whether such crashes happen often enough to make all the gold.

open_questions.q: How long does plastic really last in the sea and soil?
open_questions.why_open: Most plastic has existed for less than a human lifetime. The long numbers you hear are estimates, and scientists are still measuring how fast it breaks into smaller bits.

open_questions.q: How did the hand-spinners of Bengal make Dhaka muslin so fine?
open_questions.why_open: The skill was lost in the 1800s. People today are trying to bring back the special cotton plant and the spinning skill, and they are still finding out how it was done.

open_questions.q: Could we make strong materials the way living things do, like spider silk?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists understand parts of how spiders spin silk, but nobody can yet make spider silk as well as a spider, in large amounts.

open_questions.q: Should we name a new age of the Earth after people, the Anthropocene?
open_questions.why_open: In 2024 the scientists who name Earth's ages voted no, for now. Many others still use the idea, and the argument goes on.

open_questions.q: Can we build bases on the Moon from Moon dust?
open_questions.why_open: Engineers have made test bricks from pretend Moon dust on Earth, but nobody has yet built anything on the Moon itself.

open_questions.q: Where exactly should the line between natural and made be drawn?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on what we mean by nature. Scientists, philosophers and different traditions give different answers.

maths.problem: One litre of sea water has about 35 grams of salt hidden in it. A salt maker dries 4 litres in a pan. About how much salt does she get?
maths.explain: Each litre gives 35 grams. 4 litres is 4 lots of 35 grams. 35 + 35 = 70. 70 + 70 = 140. So 4 × 35 = 140 grams. That is about as heavy as a small cup of salt.
maths.context: In the salt experiment, you dried salty water on a plate in the sun. Salt makers do the same in big flat pans of sea water.

answer_chart.title: Salt from sea water, at about 35 grams a litre

maths.why_maths: Salt makers need to know how much salt their pans will give. Multiplying the salt in one litre by the number of litres tells them, without waiting for the sun.

maths.problem: On the Three-Heap Walk, Meena found 7 once-living things, 4 never-living things and 5 things made by people. Draw a bar chart. How many things did she find altogether? How many were natural?
maths.explain: Altogether: 7 + 4 + 5 = 16. The natural things are the once-living and the never-living ones: 7 + 4 = 11. The bar chart has three bars: 7, 4 and 5 tall.
maths.context: On the Three-Heap Walk, you collect small things and sort them into three heaps: once-living natural things, never-living natural things, and things made by people.
maths.why_maths: A pile of things is hard to compare at a glance. A tally and a bar chart show straight away which heap is biggest.

maths.problem: Your wet clay diya weighed 120 grams. After 2 days of drying, it weighed 95 grams. How much water went into the air?
maths.explain: The clay did not go anywhere. Only the water left. So the water is the difference: 120 − 95 = 25 grams. Check: 95 + 25 = 120.
maths.context: In the From Soil to Diya project, you weighed your diya wet, just after making it, and again when it was dry.
maths.why_maths: We cannot see water leaving the clay. Weighing before and after, and taking away, shows exactly how much left.

maths.problem: Bakelite, the first plastic made completely from chemicals, was invented in 1907. Galalith, the milk plastic, was invented in 1897. How many years apart were they? How many years ago was Bakelite invented, if this year is 2026?
maths.answer: 10 years apart. Bakelite was invented 119 years ago.
maths.explain: 1907 − 1897 = 10 years. For the second part: 2026 − 1907. From 1907 to 2007 is 100 years. From 2007 to 2026 is 19 more. 100 + 19 = 119 years.
maths.context: In the milk plastic experiment, you made a plastic from milk. A factory version called Galalith was invented in 1897. Bakelite, made from chemicals, came in 1907.
maths.why_maths: Dates tell a story only when we work out the gaps. Subtracting shows that plastic is a very young material compared with clay, cotton or salt.

maths.problem: You spun a cotton thread 10 centimetres long in 1 minute. If you kept spinning at the same speed, how long would your thread be after 5 minutes? After 10 minutes?
maths.answer: 50 centimetres after 5 minutes. 100 centimetres, which is 1 metre, after 10 minutes.
maths.explain: Each minute adds 10 cm. After 5 minutes: 5 × 10 = 50 cm. After 10 minutes: 10 × 10 = 100 cm. 100 cm is 1 metre. A sari needs hundreds of metres of thread, so hand spinning takes a very long time.
maths.context: In the Spin a Thread activity, you twisted cotton fluff into thread with a pencil spindle.

answer_chart.title: Thread length at 10 cm a minute

maths.why_maths: Spinning feels slow, but how slow? Multiplying minutes by centimetres shows how much work is hidden inside every piece of cloth.

roots.context: We have been learning where every material comes from, and how people change natural materials. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

three.who_am_i: The atoms in your body were made inside stars, long ago.
three.what_is_life: Wasps make paper and silkworms make silk. Life is always making materials.
three.what_is_this_world: People never make new atoms. They only change what the Earth gives.

roots.thread: A steel spoon, a plastic bucket and a mango seem very different. Yet all are built from the same few kinds of atoms. Those atoms were made in stars. DeepKids believes this is the One becoming many: one star-stuff taking the shapes of salt, clay, silk and you. Natural and made things come from the same source.

teachings.teaching: A spider spins its thread out of itself. Plants grow up out of the earth. In the same way, everything comes out of the one unchanging source.
teachings.link: A silkworm makes silk and a wasp makes paper from inside their own bodies. The Earth, too, gives every material from itself.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, The Heart of Understanding (1988)
teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper. You can see the cloud, the rain and the tree in it. Take them away, and there is no paper.
teachings.link: Every material carries its whole story: the plant, the rock, the sea and the people who changed it.

science.text: When people cook, melt or mix materials, no atoms are made or lost. They are only rearranged.
Almost every atom in your body, apart from hydrogen, was made inside a star.

other_view.view: Charvaka taught that everything is made of four elements: earth, water, fire and air. Even awareness comes from them, and it ends when the body ends.
